Right Hon. Sir ROBERT BORDEN (Prime Minister) laid on the Table copy of Order in Council, dated 3rd September, 1917, appointing the Deputy Minister of Justice, Oliver Mowat Biggar, of the city of Edmonton; John H. Moss, of the city of Toronto; Louis Loranger, of the city of Montreal, and Lieutenant Colonel H. A. C. Machin, of the town of Kenora, Ont., a council to advise and assist in the administration and enforcement of the Military Service Act, 1917, to be known as the Military Service Council; the Deputy Minister of Justice to be chairman of the council.

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Stewart in the Chair.
Harbours and rivers-Nova Scotia-Ben Eoin-wharf, $2,200.

['I will get the explanation for my hon. friend.
Progress reported.
On motion of Hon. Mr. Reid, the House adjourned at 11.20 p.m.
Wednesday, September 5, 1917.']
Is this for the construction of a new wharf?
These small items are for repairs at different places.
When is this money to be spent?	[DOT]
As soon as the vote is passed. In some cases work is being proceeded with now.

Will the minister explain why he has dropped certain items that were in the estimates during the last few years and introduced new ones? For the last five or six years there has been in the estimates an item for a wharf at Cole harbour-which is as necessary, in my judgment, as any wharf proposed to be built on the coast of the Maritime Provinces. This item has been dropped from the estimates, and certain other items- dealing with works not nearly so important have been introduced. This is not 'an isolated case; quite a number of projected works in estimates and new items have been inNova Scotia have been dropped from the Estimates and new items have been inserted in their places without any apparent reason. Upon what principle has the minister made up these supplementary estimates?

This amount is required to construct a creosoted timber wharf 175 feet long and 16 feet wide-with a head block 20 by 30 feet-and a small warehouse thereon, 10 by 14 feet. The estimated cost is $1,634.50, made up as follows: creosoted piling, $819.60; native round logs, $25.20; dimension timber, $260; timber, plank covering, $163.20; driving and securing 40 piles, $147; sand and gravel in approach, $34.50; warehouse, $175; land, $10; total, $1,634.50; superintendence, contingencies, etc., $365.50; total, $2,000. Add ten- per cent for advance in prices of labour and material since the report was made, $200. This is really a new work; it is in the constituency of Cape Breton South.
I understood that this was a new work, and I was rather surprised at the minister saying this item was for repairs.
I was speaking about the preceding item.
We are discussing this one. I would like the minister to read the report recommending the construction of this wharf.

District Engineer Bernas-coni, in his report of March 20, 1915, says:
There are at present seven public wharves on the shores of East Bay, fairly well distributed, with the exception of the shore between Big Pond and the head of East Bay, a distance of 12 miles. The proposed wharf at Ben Eoin would be about midway between these points and would fill the gap and give the required accommodation to the inhabitants of that section of the district. The site for the proposed wharf is owned by Mr. Joseph McLellan, who offers to sell the land required for the sum of $10, which price I consider fair and lust.
That is the official information.
Will the minister explain why it is that, report having been received in 1915, no appropriation has been placed in the estimates until now?
I cannot explain that. The estimates, of course, were made out by the Minister of Public Works. These are the explanations furnished by the department, and I cannot give any others.
Does the minister think there is more money with which to build wharves this year than there was in 1914?
I am not doing any thinking on this; it is an estimate of the Department of Public Works.
If the minister is not doing any thinking, it would be a good idea for him to do some.
I am satisfied that the Minister of Public Works would not insert this item unless he thought it was absolutely necessary.
For election purposes.
No.

The Teport says that there are seven wharves already in East Bay. but inasmuch as there is a distance of 12 miles between two wharves, it is important that this wharf should be built. I very much regret that the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) is not here. He might perhaps produce the plan which he laid upon the table of this House in 1910 or 1911, and on which he had marked out the number of wharves in the Maritime Provinces built by the late Government, as he said, without any justification. This is another case in which the Government appear to have gone back
on whatever record they made, when they were in Opposition, with respect ito the expenditure of money upon wharves. I am as much interested in the convenience of the people of my district as the acting Minister of Public Works can possibly be, but the people of my district realize the necessity for economy on the part of the Government, and I beg to assure the minister that they understand why this estimate is brought before Parliament at tihe present time. A request was made three years ago for the building of a wharf at that point. That request was not complied with. Year after year went by; estimates were voted by Parliament, but no provision was made for the building of this wharf until the year 1917. If this item had been placed in the main estimates for 1917-18, the Government might stiU be entitled to some credit for discharging a public duty; but inasmuch as provision for the building of this wharf is made only in the supplementary estimates, which came down after it was determined by the Government that there should be an election, we can all realize the motive that actuated the minister. If there ever were a time when provision for expenditure on new woTk ought not to be made, it certainly ought to be now, and I would suggest-and I take all responsibility necessary for making this suggestion-that the minister drop this item out of the estimates.

I know something about the location of this wharf, and the engineer who reported to the minister that there were seven wharves in East Bay must have been seeing seven times as many wharves as he should have seen. There are not seven wharves in East Bay. Three years ago I forwarded a petition from the people at the head of East Bay to this Government asking for repairs to a wharf which has been of considerable service to the inhabitants of that place, and which is quite near East Bay church in the vicinity of which the larger proportion of the people live. The Department of Public Works paid no attention to the matter, and, as a result, that wharf is absolutely useless and worthless to the people of that section. Has the minister any plan showing how the people who would be served by this proposed wharf are going to get to the main road? It is about two and one-half miles from the main road, and there is absolutely no communication. If the minister wishes to have a wharf which will be of service to the people, he should repair that wharf which has been

allowed to go to ruin. Instead of there being seven wharves, there is one on the south side of East Bay in the constituency which I represent and another on the north side of East Bay in the constituency represented by my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie). There must be some mistake in the report.
That is too bad. So ne more wharves should be built there.

I am not complaining about this wharf. Of course, my hon. friend knows all about this wharf as he knows, or pretends to know, whether he does or not, about wharves in all parts of the country. I am simply giving to the minister information which I think he should have. I am not objecting to the item at all.
The hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) asks that this item be dropped.

If my hon. friend (Mr. Bradbury) would attend to his business and endeavour to give information to the minister as I am trying to do, he would get along very well. I do not interrupt my hon. friend when he is giving information to the minister in regard to matters in his riding. The Minister of1 Public Works should investigate this matter and take into consideration the petition sent in to the department three years ago for repairs to a wharf at the head of East Bay. Perhaps the deputy minister will remember about the petition which was signed by a large section of the inhabitants there, headed, I think, by the clergyman in charge of the parish.

I have no other information than this before me, and the officials of the department have given ,me the report of the officer in charge of that district who recommends that this wharf should be built. As I understand the hon. member, this wharf which it is proposed to be built is in his constituency.
Yes.

I have the plans here showing the proposed wharf. Do I understand the hon. member 'to say that this wharf is not required and that he wants the item struck out, because if he does I will strike it out.

If the minister will
guarantee to me that he will look at the Government wharf at the head of the south side of East Bay, and instead of spending

the money on this wharf, will spend it on repairing that wharf, which will better serve the people at Ben Eoin, I shall be satisfied.

I cannot make any such guarantee, because we cannot expend any amount on repairs on some other wharf unless the item is placed in the estimates just as this one has been. Therefore, if I strike out this item the matter of the repairs to the wharf mentioned by the hon. member will, of course, have to be taken up by the department, and if the situation is as he describes, an item can be inserted in the estimates next session.
So far as I am concerned, I would recommend the striking out of this item.
I will strike it out.
It amounts to $2,200. This wharf would not serve the public at that point at all. The minister need not think I am afraid of striking out any item that is not going to serve the people.
I am not saying that.

The engineer may have been misinformed. It would have been better had the department done as it was requested to do, namely, to make repairs to the wharf at the head of East Bay. I see no good in building a wharf at this particular place. I would be glad if the minister would show me on the plan how lie is going to get from the proposed wharf at Ben Eoin on to the main road.
The right of way is marked on the plan, showing how you can get to the wharf.
You will have to buy the right of way.	,
The man is willing to sell it for $10.
That is cheap enough.

I think the minister is mistaken when he says he has not the power to change an item in the estimates. I know for a fact that he has done it in reference to a wharf in my constituency. Prior to the defeat of the late government a sum of money was voted for the building of a wharf at Sand Point, on the Strait of Canso. AUore than that, a contract was entered into, and the material collected for the building of the wharf, but when the present government came into power their friends in that locality persuaded them to

change the site of the wharf to another place further down the Strait. The reason for making this change was that the government wanted to purchase a site from a Conservative heeler in that locality, as a reward for his political services. The wharf was built at this new location, and then it turned out that there was not enough water there to make the wharf of any service to the people. The intention was to build a v'harf at which the steamer which plies between Guysborough and Mulgrave could call, but the water is so .shallow the steamer is unable to come in, and consequently the wharf is no good to anybody. The owner of the land got his purchase price for it, and he was the only person who benefited by the expenditure of $5,000 at that point. So there is one case in which the minister changed an item in the estimates, and if he was able to change an item then, he ought tv be able to change one now for my hon. friend from South Cape Breton.
The minister has never answered my question as to the principle which is acted upon in making up the estimates. I have pointed out to him that there has been an item in the estimates for the last six years for the building of a wharf in my constituency at a point where it is very much needed. Time after time the minister and his predecessors have promised to construct the wharf. The point where this wharf is required is not in the woods, where there are no roads or people, but in a thickly settled district, and the people of *Cole Harbour, Charlos' Cove, Cashin's Cove and American Harbour have all asked that it be built. The minister has cut that item out of the estimates, and in its place has an item for the building of a wharf at Ben Eoin, where apparently there are no inhabitants and no roads to give access to the wharf. I should like the minister to tell the committee on what principle he makes these changes in the estimates.

There are, of course, many wharves in the province of Nova Scotia, and applications are coming in every year for new wharves. Some of these applications are put off from time to time, but each year the minister takes up the most pressing cases, and selects those which he thinks are the most urgent. These items are all small amounts. Personally I feel that the people who have not the advantage of railway accommodation should have the benefit of wharves, and that these should be much closer together than in the older settled parts of Canada where there are
railway facilities. I have never raised any objection, and never will, to giving the people along the Atlantic coast proper wharf accommodation. The hon. member says that he knows of a case where the money was not spent where it was intended to be spent. My information is that the department do not know of a case of that kind, nor do they understand that it is possible to change the location when the vote has specified the point at which the money must be spent. But it may happen that the engineer may move the site a hundred feet or perhaps half a mile if he thinks it will be an improvement, and that is quite within the spirit of the law.
But this money has not been voted yet.

It is in the estimates, and if the item goes through, the wharf will be constructed at that point. Possibly there may be other points in the hon. member's constituency where the need is more pressing; that is a matter of opinion. I have never been in that locality, and my hon. friend knows it better than I do, but the officials of the department down there say that that is the point where this wharf should be built.
They are not doing their duty.
A number of people live in that locality.
Not where the wharf is to be; nobody lives there at all.

Ben Eoin is situated on the southern shore of East bay, thirteen miles southwest of the city of Sydney, which is the nearest railway station. It has a population of about a hundred, whose principal occupation is farming and fishing.

My hon. friend is referring to East Bay. At Ben Eoin there are only about seven families, and if the wharf is built at that point, it will be right at the bottom of a mountain. Half a mile down the shore at East Bay, where the population is, there has been a wharf for a great many years, perhaps for half a century, and it has been kept in repair by succeeding governments.
It serves the people of East Bay, the 100 families the hon. gentleman refers to, together with the seven or eight families on the mountain of Ben Eoin, four miles from East Bay. Three or four years ago, or more, the wharf got into disrepair, and a petition was sent to the Government to have

it repaired. There was no necessity for buying land there. If the Government spend $500 on the old wharf, which is in the centre of the population, they will be serving the whole neighbourhood. I think it is unfair to the people of East Bay that this wharf should he 'built at Ben Eoin, and that the wharf in their own county should be left to go to destruction. I am taking this point in the interest of the people themselves. I know the locality almost as well as I know this Chamber. I am surprised that any engineer should say there were seven wharves in East Bay, and that this wharf i6 serving 100 families.
If we put this vote through I do not see that it can be used for repairs to a wharf at some other place,

I understood the minister to say he would strike it out, if I recommended it. I would not recommend the striking out of anything that would benefit the people in my riding. I would be a foolish man to do anything which was not beneficial to them, if I intended to go back for re-election. That is certainly logic. I am recommending this item should be struck out because it is not in the publio interest.
Then we will strike it out.

I remember something taking place about this matter when I was minister, and I remember that I was pressed to take over that old wharf and put it in repair. Does the minister think there is a prominent place in East Bay where the wharf could be properly placed? Why not insert the word "Ben Eoin wharf, at or near East Bay?" We need not strike out the item.

If the hon. gentleman thinks the wharf should not be built there I do not want to keep the item in the estimates, but I think it would be better to leave it in, and before the department would proceed with it they could look thoroughly into the matter and decide on the proper course. However, I do not think we should waste time over it, and I move that the item be struck out.
Would it be in order to make a motion to use $1,600 of this money to make improvements on the wTharf at East Bay?
No.

This vote is for the construction of a new wharf, and there are several votes under the headings " Harbours and Rivers-Nova Scotia," for new wharves. The Minister of Finance solemnly promised Parliament, on more than one occasion, during the last two years, that no new public works would be undertaken. The late Minister of Public Works also promised Parliament the same thing. 1 say that on that ground the item should be dropped. This item of $97,000 for new wharves and repairs in Nova Scotia should be struck from the estimates. Every single item of such a character should be dropped, for the reason that the money will not be expended this year. It is practically impossible to effect repairs to wharves late in the year; it will not be possible to place this work in the hands of competent men before October or November, and it will then be too late. Parliament must meet again before March 31 of next year. There will then be sufficient time to vote these moneys, and no useful purpose can be served by voting them now.

I sincerely hope the minister will not yield to request of the hon. member for Halifax. Nearly all these items are for repairs, and a dollar spent now may mean a sarving of a thousand dollars later on, and prevent a good deal of hardship.
We will attend to it next year.

The hon. gentleman says this is not the time to spend money on wharves in Nova Scotia. I desire to say that from now to the middle of November is the most feasible and practical time for such expenditure. The farmers are not very busy now, and we are having our best weather. I am absolutely astounded to hear the hon. member for Halifax objecting to a paltry expenditure of a little money for repairs to keep the wharves of that province in proper condition. I believe his statement will be received with a great deal of regret and astonishment by the people of his province.
Not at all.

I have no interest in the matter, and it makes no difference to me whether the items are struck out ox not, but I want to say that I represent a constituency three times the size of Nova Scotia, and I have a coast line three times the length and breadth of that province,

and I can assure the hon. gentleman there are no items for new works in my province, the items being all for repairs. I am very glad that the hon. gentleman did not include British Columbia in his request for cutting out the items. Oui waters are infested with teredo, which are very destructive to wharves. I have known, piles 18 inches thick to jbe cut off by teredo in British Columbia in one year. I hope the hon. gentleman from Halifax will not press, his request. When a wharf needs immediate repair it is good policy to attend to it at once, because, by spending a dollar, you save an expenditure of ten or fifteen dollars. I assure the members for the Maritime Provinces that, so far as British Columbia is concerned, there is no necessity for any arguments with regard to new wharves, because all the items in the supplementary estimates for that province are for repairs only. Practically three-quarters of the coast line in British Columbia are in my own constituency.

My only difficulty in , regard to this question is that all these repairs are required this spring. I called the attention of the Government to several works in my own county, when the general estimates were brought down, and I am surprised that the hon. gentleman from Annapolis did not protest then that these items were not contained in the main Estimates, because, if they had been in thosg estimates, there would be some hope of having the money spent this year.

The general estimates were
made out last October.

I can tell the hon.
gentleman that, so far as my county is concerned, all the works provided for in the supplementary estimates were necessary, and this money was required four years ago. The Government has failed, year after year, to put one dollar in the estimates for repairs in the county of Inverness. I can assure the hon. gentleman that all the works in Nova Scotia are in the same position. Here we have $18,000 for repairs -and improvements for Margaree harbour. I succeeded in getting the Public Works Department to look after this important public work in Margaree, but if it had been attended to four years ago an expenditure of $1,800 additional to the amount expended would have been sufficient. I protested against the failure of the Government to look after it, and to-day
we have $18;000 in the estimates to repair the destruction which has occurred in the last four years. The Government cannot say that they did not know the conditions in that district because I warned them continually year after year for four or, five years. I believe they repeatedly found this in that one instance.
There is another item for Port Hood wharf. There is a wharf which-cost this country about $40,000 and the Government let this wharf go into decay and destruction year after year, for five years. I pointed out to the department how this work was going to decay. Neither the Minister of Public Works nor the Government paid any atteention to my warning. The surprise to me is that at this moment, preceding an election, 'I find $6,000 to do a work of repair that will cost -about $35,000 or $40,000. I find the same conditions along the coast from one end of the county to the other. There are seven or eight votes that cannot be spent this fall with any reasonable results, and -the work o-f destruction is going on all the time. Every fall, for the last four years, when (there has been any -agitation around Mar

gane-e with respect to municipal politics, or something of that kind, you would find a dozen of men at work in October or November. The foreman was getting his full time although he did -not put in more -than forty-eight hours a week. I find no fault with the foreman, under the circumstances he could do no better. 'This- was going on during October and November. I told the Minister of Public Works that that was an awfully poor way of spending the money. If they -attempt to get -any work done along our coast after September they cannot [DOT]get -good results. If the foreman were authorized -early to go to work he could get honest results. The timber is grow'ing in the woods yet.

Will my hon. friend
allow me

?
Mr. -CHISHOLM : No, I am -not done yet. Let my hon. friend possess his soul in patience and not be in so much of a hurry. With regard to the work which is provided for here, if the minister will give me the -assurance that they will go on with the work immediately, I will -point out several expenditures that he might get results from. But, I anticipate that it will be impossible. 'The Department of Public Works have not the machinery at work to enable them to- put the material out before October. If they cannot get the men



at work by October it is a crime to spend the money there.
Does the hon. gentleman advocate striking out the items in so far as they' appertain to the county of Inverness?

My hon. friend in this thinks he is smart. I advocated for the last five years that expenditures should be made every year in order to preserve the public works in Inverness. Had the Government acted upon my advice they would not have had to expend within 20 per cent of the money that they will now have to expend to put these works in repair. I am not particularly worried as to whether we leave these items in the estimates or not if I have not the assurance of the minister that they will be spent because this Parliament will meet again next winter and whether we have these items in the supplementary estimates now or whether they are in the estimates when this Parliament meets next winter, makes very little difference. But, the hon. gentleman does not think I am silly enough to ask that any of these items be struck out. 1 have been advocating for the last five years that these works should be kept in repair.

The hon. gentleman
thinks I must be under the impression that I am smart because I asked him to answer a plain, straightforward question. I hope nothing I have said will indicate that I have any great conceit or that I think I am particularly smart. I would think it a fair inference to be drawn that when items are inserted in the estimates, and when an hon. gentleman who is usually silent, gets up and protests, he must want them struck out. That is the only inference I can draw and I am afraid I cannot get very much light from his answer. If hon. gentleman opposite had not consumed so much of the time of this Parliament, if they had allowed the business to proceed more expeditiously, these items would have been passed several months ago and the money would have been available in the early summer. But, I cannot agree with the hon. gentlemen when he says it is impracticable to spend any money this fall. October is a very desirable month in which to spend money. The hon. gentleman seems to be incensed because certain expenditures have been provided for and yet the moment these items are placed in the estimates they meet with a protest from the desk mate of

the hon. gentleman. I can understand why the Government might be a little reluctant to make expenditures in Nova Scotia when the members sitting for these seats themselves are the first to get up and protest. We had a case this afternoon. There is in the estimates an item for .Cape Breton county and a protest against it comes from the hon. member who represents that county. Then, when we come to an item for Inverness county, the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) vehemently protests against any item of that kind being inserted in the estimates at any time during the period of the war. I think hon. gentlemen can hardly expect the Government to be very liberal when their action in this respect meets with so much opposition from hon. gentlemen opposite. If the hon. member for Inverness is anxious to have money spent in his county o.n needed repairs he should desist from criticism of the expenditures.

I do not want my hon. friend (Mr. Davidson) to create the impression that I protest against these items.. I protest against the idea of placing these items in the -supplementary estimates when it will be impossible to spend the tfioney this fall. And my hon. friend should be able to- understand plain English before he undertakes to put questions which cannot do more than expose his lack of common understanding. I protested that these items should have been contained in the general or supplementary estimates of last year, the year before and the year before that so that something could be- accomplished. My hon. friend twits me because I am not heard very often in this House. I am heard whenever occasion demands it and the interests of my county need attention and my country in my judgment needs my opinion.
No, not at all. I did not mean that my hon. friend was not heard from often.

He is surprised that men like myself who do not often address this House should get up and offer any criticism to items of this kind. The business of this House would be expedited if there were more members like myself and if they possessed a little particle of modesty.
I could not agree to strike out any of these items.

I must protest again; I never asked it. He desires to put me in a false light. I want every item and ten

times as many and t-he need of Inverness requires it.

At any rate the hon. junior member for Halifax said that he thought that they should be all struck out. I am not referring to the hon. member for Inverness. The main estimates were made up in October. These items were all taken up during the winter and this list has been made out. In making out the list of these repairs, the officials of the department take the reports of the engineers in the district and collect the ones that in their opinion are the most urgent. I believe that every hon. member, no matter on what side of the House he is, will admit that the repairs on the list are actually required at the places which are named.
Certainly.

The Minister of Public Works, in selecting the places thought to be most urgent, did not select all the places where repairs might be done. He has taken wharves in Inverness, Cape Breton, Cumberland and other counties and he was very fair in making his selection. I agree that there are many other wharves which probably require repairs but some of them are not so urgent as others. Under the circumstances it does strike me that the hon. member should allow these small amounts to go through. As far as completing these repairs is concerned, hon. members know that the amounts are small.
There is no reason why any one of these votes could not be spent this fall; they are for small repairs, and it would surely be better, if these wharves require repairs, that they' should be made and that the people should have the benefit.

The minister having
struck out the item for Ben Eoin wharf, to which I objected, I am in accord with everything else that is proposed to be done in my county. The new wharf at Grand Mira is an absolute necessity, and so are all the repairs to wharves in Cape Breton county.
T think it would have been better to have left the vote for Ben Eoin wharf in and to have carried on the work if possible.

The hon. member for Inverness (Mr. Chisholm) has made a serious charge against the department: that although he called attention to the need of inexpensive repairs to the breakwater at Margaree harbour five years ago, nothing
337*
was done, and the breakwater has been so damaged that it is now necessary to spend this large amount of $18,000 to make the repairs. If that is true, it is criminal neglect, and some one ought to be held accountable for it.

Frequently, when statements of that kind have been made in this House, I have found from the reports of the engineers that they are not well founded. The hon. member may possibly have had a report from some one in the locality who wanted a little work.

When I make a statement I generally know what I am talking about. I live within half a mile of this wharf, and, when the weather is fine, I go down there about once a day. I have gone out of my way to get all the information necessary. I have written the department and interviewed the minister in regard to this work many times, and it will be news to the people of that locality that the minister thinks that right treatment has been given to that public work for the last five years. I venture to say that $38,000 will not fully repair that wharf. In 1911 there was a vote of $10,000 in the general estimates to be spent there, but it was not spent. Small sums were spent each year, in October and November when results could not be accomplished, and that has been the great difficulty.
I have looked at the official explanation of this vote, and my hon friend seems to be quite mistaken. This $18,300 is not to repair a breakwater.
I did not say that nor could I, because I do not know yet what it is for.

He was arguing on the assumption that it was for the breakwater. It is for repairing the breakwater; but, in addition to that, it is for the building of a proposed sand groin 550 feet long and 15 feet wide, a new work entirely.
Is this new work a war time work?

The hon. member for the county will agree that it is necessary to repair this breakwater. The sand groin is erected opposite the breakwater
4 p.m. to protect it from the action of the waves.
It is not to protect the country from the Huns is it?

I am glad my Ron. friend takes an interest in protecting the country from the Huns, and if this breakwater or any other will prevent the Huns from landing there, I am sure every member will support it.
We are told there would be no new works during the war.

This is repairing an old
work. I am sure the hon. member for the county will agree that this sand groin is necessary to protect the breakwater. This sand groin is to be 550 feet long and 15 feet wide, and the estimated cost is $7,500. In addition to that, there is an item for dredging the channel at the entrance, $6,000, which is not applied to work on the breakwater. I mention this only to show that the hon. member did not understand the nature of the vote.
The committee has been discussing the item of Margaree harbour, which we have not yet reached. It would be better if this discussion was discontinued and resumed when the proper item is called.
The hon, member for South Cape Breton says that the item now under consideration is not necessary; we will strike it out.
When an engineer of the department makes a report and the minister accepts it, is it the policy of the department to throw out the item simply because a member says that the work is unnecessary?

The member for South Cape Breton knows the locality; he says that this work is unnecessary because there is another wharf about a mile from the place where this wharf is proposed to be constructed. He says that this wharf would serve only seven or eight families. Under the circumstances, pending further investigation, I am willing that the item be struck out.
Does t'he hon. gentleman not ask that the old wharf be repaired?
Yes, but I cannot change a vote for the construction of a wharf to a vote for repairs to another wharf a mile away.

The report of t'he engineer shows that the wharf is really intended to be at East Bay. The report says that there are one hundred families where this pro-

posed wharf is to be built; the one hundred families are at East Bay, not at Ben Eoin. The member for South Cape Breton does not want a wharf constructed half a mile or so from a settled district where there are a large number of families and where there is already a wharf, although it is in bad repair. If you build a wharf half a mile away from a settled district you create division of opinion in the community; the tendency is to take the business away from the settlement and to establish a little community in a new place, which is extremely objectionable. I have always endeavoured to see that the necessary public accommodation was afforded in-the settled localities.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have no motion before me with reference to this item. The minister .simply said that he was willing to strike it out.
Mr. Chairman, I will make a motion.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I cannot receive a
motion from the hon. gentleman.
I move that the item be struck out.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I was mistaken; I had something else in my mind at that moment.

Motion agreed to, and item struck out.
Boularderie Centre-repairs to wharf, $625.
['I was mistaken; I had something else in my mind at that moment.']

I have no doubt that these repairs are quite necessary; I know the wharf well. A good deal of money has been spent upon a wharf at New Campbell-ton, but the work has never been completed. What was expended will go to waste unless something be done to keep the wharf in repair and to complete the work. I would suggest that the minister get a report on the matter.

I shall bring the matter to the attention of the department and have the information placed on record when the estimates for next session are being considered. They are generally considered in the month of October.
If the minister could get a little money to put that wharf in repair, he should not wait until next year.
We might take it out of the general vote.

Mr. Bernasconi, the
government engineer at North Sydney, could report on it. New Campbellton is only a sihort distance from the town of North Sydney.
Cow bay (Port Morien)-repairs to breakwater, $1,800.
Mr.' REID:	Assistant District Engineer
Cooper reported on February 6, 1917, as follows:
The face-timbers on inner side of the head block have been eaten away and the bays back of this face have had the ballast washed out by the under-tow that continually heaves around the corner. The covering and stringers on the outer head are also In a bad condition and to repair this part X beg to recommend placing a concrete block, 25 feet in length and of the dimensions shown on the accompanying plan and in placing a concrete covering over the outer head block.
Was any money spent on this work this year?
No.

During the last few
years an amount of money has been spent there every summer in extending the breakwater. The tidal water is very strong there; it has been found necessary, to put concrete wings on the breakwater.

My memorandum shows that this breakwater was built by the owners of the Gowrie coal mine on the north side of the bay, and came under the charge of the department in 1873. It originally extended 1,347 feet, to 17 feet at low or to 23 feet at high water, and was about 44 feet in width. The .area of the basin enclosed between it and the shipping pier of the Gowrie mines, now the property of the Dominion Coal Company, was 17 acres, 10 acres of which had a depth of from 9 to 17 feet at low water. The breakwater was seriously damaged during the gale of August 24, 1873. Large expenditures have been made from time (to time in extending and repairing the work. During the year ending March 31, 1915, the sum of $4,075.76 was expended in completing the placing of concrete blocks for the protection of the seaward face of the work. Work was done by day labour During the year ended March 31, 1916, the. sum of $1,850.54 was expended by day labour on procuring a derrick with winch and in constructing and placing large concrete blocks along the seaward face of the breakwater, over a distance of 53 feet,
thereby completing the concrete blocks' protection on the seaward face of the breakwater.

This is a work that
should be una-r,taken Tight away. It is in a sort of a basin in which the wind does not have much effect, and if the work were undertaken now, it could be finished this fall.

The work will be undertaken as soon as the estimate is passed.
Cribbin's Point-repairs to wharf, $1,500.
When is it proposed to do this work?

There should not be any
trouble to do this work within the next two or three months. The work is to be done by day labour; $1,004 out of the $1,500 is for timber and planking, and $200 is for removal of old work.

Has the material been
purchased?	[DOT]
No.
No part of the money has been expended up to date?

No money has been spent
because the estimate -has not yet been passed, but the intention is to go to work at once on all these small works in these different localities.

What has become of a number of other items for works in the county of Antigonish? I cannot say from memory the names .of all the places, but a list of them has been put before the House several times by Mr. William Chisholm the former member. They were voted some years ago for the purpose of carrying a local election in that constituency. They were repeated in the estimates for a number of years, and they have now disappeared altogether. Does the minister ever intend to renew those items?

I think the Minister of Public Works explained', on the main estimates that he had dropped a long list of items for new work that he did not consider it necessary to proceed with during the present season. I suppose the items mentioned by the hon, members were among those that disappeared in that way.
Eastern harbour (Cheticamp) retaining wall,
This is required to construct a dry rubble retaining wall asked for by the fishermen.

I have been advocating this work for some time. It is very desirable.
Fourchu-extension of wharf, $4,200.

When is this work to be
undertaken?
As soon as the item is passed.
Is it intended to extend the wharf further out into the harbour?
We are going to raise and extend the wharf.

How far is it to be extended? What is more important than raising the wharf is to have some dredging done there, so as to- enable a steamer to call at the wharf. When the wharf was purchased in 1911, it was intended that the steamer which serves the southern shore of Halifax and Cape Breton should call at the wharf for the purpose of giving the residents of that important community connection with their markets east iand west. Unfortunately, since the change of Government, no improvement has been made in that harbour up to the present time. Considerable dredging was done before 1911, but more is necessary at the approach to the wharf. These people are without any communication with the outside world, as the sailing vessel which used to call there was lost some years ago, and they now have to depend entirely upon a small steamer owned by a private company that operates during the lobster season between Fourchu and Louisburg. I would urge the Government to take a portion of the money which is to be voted under the head of dredging in the Maritime Provinces, and do some further dredging in the neighbourhood of the wharf, to give the people in that locality the same advantages that are enjoyed by other ports in the province. It is one of the most important fishing communities in the province of Nova Scotia, and the people are severely handicapped by having no means of exporting their fish to the markets to which fish caught in other parts of the province are shipped. I am very glad indeed to see the Government is going to extend the wharf, but they should not stop there, because extending the wharf will not be sufficient. Some dredging is absolutely necessary in order to give a sufficient depth of water to enable these steamers to call there.	.	[DOT]

I see by the report that this is a very important matter for the people in that locality, as they are forty miles away

from a railway, and depend entirely on one schooner to carry their fish to Halifax. I shall draw my hon. friend's statement to the attention of the officials, and will see if any dredging can be done.
Friar's Head-repairs to breakwater, $1,000.
How much has been spent on repairs to this work the last couple of years?
The breakwater was built of concrete in the year 1901-03, and was 110 feet long, 4. feet on top, and 6 feet on bottom. The total expenditure to March 31, 1916, has been $3,773.76.

The engineer reported in 1911 that $2,200 or $2,500 was required to make the repairs to this breakwater. This money was provided in the general estimates of 1911 by the late government and should have been spent by the present Government if they had an honest desire to preserve this important public work; but then the Conservative party came into power and very few repairs have since been made. They would not even allow to be spent the amounts provided by the Liberal party. They permitted the work to go to destruction and decay. The destruction of the breakwater has continued right up to to-day, and I find that the same engineer now says that $1,000 will cover the repairs necessaray there. I cannot quite understand that. I know that $1,000 will not begin to do the repairs. I should like to know what particular part of the work is going to be repaired. The repairs are very necessary and should have been made long ago, in order to preserve the work already done there.

The figures are as follows: 1,200 ft. B.M. scantling for forms at $30, $36; 800 ft. B.M. boards: $30, $24; 3,000 lbs. steel rods reinforcement at .06, $180; 70 cu. yds. concrete at $10, $700; add for omissions and contingencies, $60; total, $1,000.
That does not complete the work.
I do not think so.

It is only $1,000 out of the $3,500 that was granted in 1911 by the Liberal government. That is to say, this Government are giving only $1,000 six years aftej they came to power out of the $3,500 provided by the Liberal party in 1911.
It is all that is being done this year.

The other $2,500 has not been spent.
Gabarus-extension of protection works, $750.

This is a very important fishing station. But for the protection works the fishermen of Gabarus would have great difficulty in getting their boats in and out of the harbour, if harbour you can call it. I have been in communication with the representative men of Gabarus, and I know they expected a much larger sum than this to be spent on the extension of the protection works. If it was only some small improvements that were required, $750 might be sufficient, tout I think the minister will agree with me that only a very small extension can toe made for that sum. The protection is required for the boats passing in and out of the harbour. The fishermen are -also having difficulty with the sand filling up the channel.
I understand that $250 has already been spent this year on urgent repairs. This $750 is all that it is proposed to spend during the present season.
What does the engineer's report say?

- In a report dated March 30, 1915, District Engineer Bernasconi states that the beach protection! work built has proved very beneficial to the harbour, but it does not extend far enough to protect the whole of the harbour, and it is now asked that it be extended a further distance of 500 feet in a southerly direction. As the work is necessary for the protection of the harbour, he recommends its construction.
There is no question as to the necessity for this work, but I think $750 will scarcely Ibuild 750 feet.
It will build a piece of it.

A very short piece. I
should like the department to get a further report from the engineer. I understand that the channel is fast filling in, and that the fishermen have great difficulty in getting their boats in and out of the harbour.
Grand Mira-wharf, $1,000.

This amount is required to construct a block and span wharf, 70 feet in length and 16 feet wide, with an "L" at the outer end 20 x 20 feet, and extending to 8 feet at low water, also warehouse 12 x 14 feet thereon.
This is a new wharf?
Yes.
Does it say on what side of the Grand Mira river?

It is asked for on Grand Mira North.
Half Island Cove-repairs to breakwater, $700.

This amount is asked for
by District Engineer Millidge to reconstruct the outer face of the breakwater at the inner end, estimated cost $700. The work is required to prevent further damage to the breakwater during the fall storms.
Is that amount considered sufficient to put the breakwater in good repair?
That is what he reports.
Has the engineer made any report in regard to another breakwater in the locality? I understood there was an application for a breaikwater on the other side, at Half Island cove.
That may be, hut that would be new work, and we are only taking items for repairs.
Does the minister intend to make the repairs this year?
Yes, we will proceed with them immediately the vote is passed.

The wharf is in a dangerous condition at present. It is in a very exposed place, and in storms the whole sweep of the bay is breaking against it. It is in such a condition that it may not stand through the winter, if some repairs are not made to it, and I am glad to know the minister is taking some steps in regard to this wharf, as it is an important wharf for that locality. If the work is not done soon it may be all carried away.
Mr. REID. We could not proceed with it until the vote was passed. The deputy had instructions to proceed with all these works at once.
Inverness harbour-repairs and improve-merits, $5,500.

This amount is asked for by District Engineer Bernasconi to effect the following improvements: (a) Repairs to western breakwater, $1,000;	(b) Dredging
the entrance channel and extending th eastern breakwater, $4,500.

Can the minister tell me what amount of work has been done? They have been doing a little work there this summer. Will the hon. gentleman tell us the nature of the work, and the amount of money already expended?
We have not a record of the work that has been done this summer. I will obtain the information.
This $5,500 is for the purpose of continuing the work that has been commenced this summer?
Yes.
Does the minister propose building any new structures there this fall?

We will proceed with what this vote provides for. It is for repairs' to western breakwater, $1,000; dredging entrance to channel and extending the eastern breakwater, $4,500. The eastern breakwater and the repairs to the western breakwater will bo commenced at once. There is a little dredging in connection with that.
What is the nature of the dredging? How does the minister propose to have it done?

The fishermen and inhabitants of Inverness request that a channel be dredged or excavated across the beach into Mclsaac's lake, to a depth of one foot at low water spring tides, fifteen feet wide on the bottom. To dredge such a channel, fifteen feet wide on bottom to a depth of one foot at low water spring tides, would require the removal of about 4,000 cubic yards from situ, to which add 25 per cent for filling in during storms-, or a total of 5,000 cubic yards.
The eastern breakwater as it now stands is 652 feet long, and the bottom, at the outer end, is about 1} feet above low water spring tides. This breakwater should be extended out 175 feet so that when completed there will be at least one foot of water at low water spring tides at the outer end.
I would suggest that a Channel, 15 feet wide on bottom, about 1,100 feet long, be excavated to a depth of one foot below low water spring tides, by horses and scrapers, and that while this work is in progress the eastern breakwater be extended 175 feet long, 15 feet wide, by building a native timber cribwork breakwater, filled with stone ballast, sheathed with native timber and covered with three-inch spruce covering.

The cost of the proposed improvement- is estimated at 14,500, made up as follows:
5,000 cu. yds. dredging at 30 c., $1,500; breakwater extension, 26,250 cu. ft. breakwater at 10 c., $2,625; add for omissions and contingencies, $375; estimated cost of extension, $3,000; total $4,500.

This work was undertaken seven years ago, and a very considerable amount of money was spent. A very substantial structure was built on the eastern side by creoso-ted timber, the intention being to open up a channel to enable schooners and steamers that ply along our coast to enter. When this Government came into power there was a considerable quantity of that creo-soted timber on the eastern side, intended to be used in continuing the work then in progress, viz., the building of breakwaters on the eastern and western -sides of the entrance, and if I am rightly informed that timber is covered with stones and sand and is not available without, a great deal of difficulty, all the results of the indifference of this Government and their absolute neglect of public property, but I qiuestion Very 'seriously whether the fishermen of Inverness are satisfied with a depth of one foot of water even at low tide. I do not see the sense of it for a moment. The depth of water contemplated -by the original surveying was, I think, ten feet at low tide. The work was initiated with a view of having that depth of water, *and all the work done by the late -Government is evidence of the intention of the late Government. This is, I suppose, one of.the most exposed portions of the province of Uova Scotia, and to think that a depth of one foot of water, at the expenditure the -minister proposes to make there, is going to be of any lasting benefit appears silly to anybody who knows anything at all about cost. In the first place, if he contemplates doing -this work this fall, after the middle of next month he can only work perhaps two or three days in a week, and the work he will accomplish to-day will be destroyed to-morrow, unless he extends that breakwater to the distance contemplated by the late Government. It will be much better to continue the original plan, get that creosoted timber the Government- succeeded in losing through some official's neglect, and put it where it was intended to go first by way of extending this breakwater, which would not cost this country but a small amount compared with the buying of the useless Quebec -and Saguenay railroad or many other indefensible expenditures.

When the Government have accomplished that they can go to work in a common-sense way and do the dredging but to think you are going to dredge a harbour with a couple of teams of horses and a scraper on the north shore of Inverness, is to me an evidence of the weaknese and absolute lack of business qualities of the department and Government. To me it would be as sensible to throw that money in the fire as far as results are concerned. The Government cannot be serious in the handling of this harbour work at Inverness, and I am sure the engineers who advise the Government expenditure of money at the entrance of Inverness harbour in the months of October and November for the purpose of deepening the channel one foot should be inmates of a lunatic asylum, rather than in charge of government works. This is one of the most important harbours on the whole coast of Inverness or the coast of any other county east of Halifax. The town of Inverness is very prosperous, an industrial town of 3,000 souls where a first-class market is available for a quantity of our fishermen's catch, but besides that it is the northern terminus of the Inverness railroad and first-class opportunity is afforded for the fresh fish business with the markets of Canada and the United States. Off this coast we find one of the best fishing grounds in Canada, or I might say, in the world. There are great prospects there for a first-class fishing industry. I have been endeavouring to point this out to the Government for the last five years. In 1911 we had $15,000 in the estimates and a provision made in the general vote for dredging of $42,000. Had that . money been spent in 1911 *; nd 1912 we would have had established perhaps one of the finest fishing industries in Canada, and would give employment to hundreds of our industrious and ambitious young men who could earn a splendid livelihood and would place within the reach of our country the very best of food-fresh fish in the very best of condition at a reasonable-price, which is so necessary at present in view of the tremendous increase in the cost of living. We all know the importance of fish to-day.
Why was it not expended in 1911?

Because the right
party, the friends of the labouring men, were not in power.

I am not speaking of the expenditure made before September,
1911. Why did the party then in power leave this till October? _

The fact is that the Government that was defeated in September, 1911, was carrying on the work of building the piers and had brought there a very large quantity of creosoted timber so as to be in a position to continue this work. The work was in progress in 1911 until the defeat of the late Government. When the party, which is the friend of the poor people, was in power, it continued the work until it went out. Then the friends of my hon. friend opposite came into power and they lost this timber by allowing it to be covered with sand. They did not continue the work for which the late Government provided the money, but allowed the money votes to lapse and never made any attempt to resume the work until now an election is imminent. The timber is there yet. In place of being put where the Liberal party contemplated it was going to be put, that is in the breakwaters, my hon. friends left it there and allowed the sand to cover it. It will cost almost as much to recover that timber as to buy new timber. Now, in the dying moments of this Parliament, to put in a small vote of $5,500 is, in my judgment, bordering on silliness, because they cannot accomplish anything practical with that vote so late in the season. However, as far as it goes, we will be grateful even for small favours, and if they will only expend this money in continuing the work initiated by the late Government, with a view of having substantial and lasting results, it will be continued by gentlemen opposite or by this side of the House as the country may determine in the near future. But I cannot characterize the idea of deepening the channel by one foot as anything but silliness, and a very striking exemplification of the business calibre of the present Government.
The hon. gentleman is hardly right when he suggests that nothing has been done by this Government. I find that previous to 1911 a small amount had been expended each year.
Where?

In 1908-09, $3,012 was expended; in 1910-11	$13,000, in 1911-12
$3,782.77, and in 1912-13, $2,596.90. Now we are going to expend more.

We had to fight Mackenzie and Mann for a number of years before we could get the land expropriated.


The vigorous and unrelenting efforts of my predecessor, the late Dr. McLennan, resulted in securing for the county the lands to enable the work to begin. When we went out of power we had all the machinery to continue this work in a vigorous way. If the Liberal party had been returned to power in 1911 they would have proceeded with this work. They provided the necessary money not only for the breakwater but for the dredging, and had secured a very considerable quantity of creosoted timber and were carrying on the work in a manner which assured a substantial structure and the creation of a satisfactory harbour for Inverness.
Irish Cove - reconstruction of wharf- $2,700.
This work is recommended by the district engineer. The money is to be used to construct a new block at the outer end of the present pier 40 x 20 feet by 14 feet high. The estimated cpst is $2,700.
Will this be done by day labour?
Yes.
Under the supervision of the engineer?
Yes.

When this wharf was being built we had a very capable man in that district to look after the work under the district engineer. I refer to Mr. Malcolm McNeil who lives quite near the wharf. I would recommend to the minister that before looking for anybody else to act under the supervision of the engineer he would endeavour to find out the capacity of Malcolm McNeil.
I will do that.
When did the minister receive the report from the engineer asking for this expenditure?
I have not the date here.

I think the minister will find it extremely difficult- to get the work done this fall. It is rather unfortunate that these amounts were not placed in the main estimates so that the work could have been done in the. early part of the season when it could have been done to advantage.
Jamesville-repairs to breakwater, $1,800.

On this item I think 1 must have a heart to heart talk with *the minister. The estimates of 1910-11 con-

tained a very substantial amount for a breakwater at Jamesville. There is a report from the engineer on file recommending the height and depth of water at the outer end of the breakwater and the general dimensions. Before a dollar of the money was spent there was a change of Government. There is a letter in the department from Mr. McCormick, who used to be my opponent, recommending that this expenditure should not be made. It was dropped and there was nothing done. The minister will find that letter in the department. It was written some time in the fall of 1911 by my good friend Mr. McCormick. I am not finding fault with what he said. Possibly that was his judgment. But, later on, there was a local election in the county of Victoria and gentlemen from outside of the county came in and the announcement was made to the people of Jamesville that although Mr. McCormick had recommended that the breakwater should not be built, something would be done. A second report, now in the minister's department, was obtained from the same engineer recommending a very much smaller amount of money and a very inferior piece of work. They started with that expenditure and they have been doing something for the last two or three years. A frail structure was put into the water and a good deal of money was expended with the result that last fall, when a considerable southwestern breeze was blowing, the whole thing took a notion that it would not stay in the water any longer. It came ashore. The minister, if he went to Jamesville, would find it high and dry, suitable only for kindling wood, at the top of the beach. I would ask the minister to let this item stand until he brings down the reports. This [DOT] is an important work and it should have been done right from the beginning. Putting this small amount of money it is merely money thrown away. If he starts with $1,800 to gather these matchwood pieces from the beach and put the structure out again it will simply come ashore. If the minister will refer to the reports in this department he will find that what I say is correct. It will be very much better to save the $1,800 and to put twice that-amount in the estimates so as to provide something that will be of some benefit to the people.
This vote is in accordance with the recommendation of Assistant District Engineer Cunningham. From his report it would seem that something should lie done, if only to protect the present work.

I am as anxious as any member to Rave money spent in my riding, and I never object to that; but I must, in all conscience, tell the minister that this thing is absolutely useless. The minister will find that when, Mr. Bernasconi was asked to make a second report for a certain amount ot money he reported that anything that could be erected for the amount specified would not stand, and: what he predicted has come to pass. I would not do justice to the people of Jamesville if I was a party to the rebuilding of this disgraceful thing, which was erected for the miserable consideration [DOT]of trying to get a few votes in that by-election. If this $1,800 is spent in this way it -will be against my will, because after what has been put there it is practically throwing the money into, the water. The only effective measure will 'be to begin anew and erect a proper breakwater there.

The objection to striking it out is that Mr. Cunningham reports that the work is necessary to protect what is already there. I feel that we should pass the item on the understanding that no work will be done without a thorough investigation by tlie department, and, of course, the engineers will visit the work in their official capacity.

If this should not 'be a sufficient amount to properly complete the work, we might be able to help out from the general vote. Tliere is no desire on the part of the department to spend any money unless the engineers assure the department that the work will be permanent.

The original plan is in the department, and if they build according to that there will be some good result.
Jones harbour - repairs to breakwater-wharf, $1,000.

This vote is asked for by District Engineer Lock to make repairs that are absolutely urgent and necessary at this place at -which there is greatly increased shipping.
L'Ardoise-repairs to breakwater, $2,600.
This vote is asked for by Mr. Bernasconi to repair several bad breaks caused by windstorms.
What is the date of that report?
June, 1917.
That is another work that cannot be done this year, as it is -at one of the most exposed places on the southern coast of Cape Breton, and any work to be effective should be done early in the season.

These estimates can he used until the latter part of April, so that it may be done in the spring.
Lingan-repairs to beach protection works, $650.
This is asked for by the district engineer to make urgent repairs and to raise the beach prolection work to the proper height, which is necessary to the permanence of this work.

I think I noticed last summer that much of this brush work had been washed away, or else had sunk into the sand. It has served a useful purpose, as similar work on other beaches
5 p.m. has done. This $650, if it is sufficient, will serve a useful purpose in keeping the road intact.
Malagash-repairs to wharf, $1,000.

When the ice was breaking
up this spring there were exceptionally heavy storms and the wharf at Malagash was considerably damaged. This is to effect the necessary repairs.
Were any petitions sent to the Department of Public Works from the New Waterford fishermen with regard to the necessity for some protection to enable them to do fishing there?

I will make a note of that
and send the hon. member a letter explaining the matter.
Mr. 'CARROLL:	I have received letters
from two or three fishermen there in regard to this matter and I told them that when the estimates were up I would bring it to the attention of the Government. I think that the department sent ia man, down there; I do not know what report he made as to the feasibility of establishing some kind of small harbour for the fishermen. I should like the minister also to give consideration to the matter of repairs at East Bay. If lie could obtain some money from the general vote for harbours and rivers, dredging, etc., in Nova Scotia, I wish he would take the necessary steps to repair that wharf. At that place they have a
?3 to

steamer service twice a week, but it is almost impossible to land anything at the East Bay wharf. I would suggest that the department get Mr. Bernasconi to make a report on the matter. They do land certain supplies there in small boats, but that operation takes a good deal of time, and the steamers have only a short time within which to make the trip.

I have asked the deputy
minister to read Hansard to-morrow and take note of what the hon. gentleman has said.
Margaree harbour-repairs and improvements, $18,300.
I am anxious to get a little more information on this item. Will the minister give me an idea of how this $18,300 is to be expended?

The amount of $18,300 is required to make the following repairs and improvements to Margaree harbour: (a) construction of sand groin and block, $7,500; (b) repairs and strengthening of breakwater, $4,800; (c) dredging channel and entrance, $6,000; total, $18,300. Tie sand groin, consisting of crib work, will be 15 feet wide on top, extending seaward from the beach, a distance of 550 feet towards the outer end of the breakwater with a solid timber block with creosoted timber substructure, 30 by 30 feet, on top at its outer end; estimated cost, $7,500. During the heavy gales which visited the western coast of Cape Breton Island in December last, a section of the breakwater at Margaree was badly wrecked and in order to prevent a breach through the work it is necessary to repair and strengthen the damaged portion as soon as possible after the opening of navigation in the spring.

This programme is in line with what was suggested five years ago, as can be seen in the reports in the minister's department. That was my own suggestion after consulting my fishermen; $10,000 was appropriated for extending the wharf and breakwater, and an [DOT] additional amount of $24,000 for dredging. I approve the plan that is to be acted upon; I think the only solution of our difficulties down there is the building of this crib work to the west of the harbour, running at an angle towards the end of the eastern breakwater. But I repeat that the expenditure of $4,500 this fall will do nothing more than perpetuate the conditions that have obtained there during the last five years. The minister proposes to expend this mere pittance to make a partial repair of the breakwater,

and lie is going to leave that structure in such condition that it will be further damaged this winter and next spring. He cannot hope, even if he economically expended this amount of $4,800, to make proper repair of the breakwater. I want to impress upon the minister the fact that this $4,500 will not make the necessary repairs on that eastern breakwater; that is, it will not place the breakwater in the condition that it was in five years ago. The report of the engineer makes reference to the fact that a portion of that breakwater was carried away last fall. The engineer has not made a full report of the conditions in respect of the rest of the breakwater, which is gradually being destroyed. The engineer took care-I do not know why -not to explain that the portion of the breakwater carried away last fall was the work done only the fall before. The new' work was carried away, and it took with it another portion of the breakwater. And I will say this, that if the engineer had consulted his foreman who did the work he would have been informed of the absurdity of the course followed by the engineer. The foreman's judgment, in my opinion, was better than the engineer's with respect to this repair work. If the minister wants anything like a proper repair of the breakwater, he must repair it in such a way that the work will be substantially done and will withstand the storms. The trouble with the work done last fall was that the spikes failed to hold because of their having been driven into old decayed wood making up that portion of the breakwater to which the new work was attached. The old work had been left gradually to fall into decay through the evident indifference of the engineer or the department, or both. In order properly to repair this breakwater, work must be begun at the bottom. If the minister proceeds as the department lias proceeded during the last three or four years, he will simply furnish a number of fishermen with firewood next spring, made up of the wood that he is going to buy, at a good price, no doubt, and put into that breakwater. The expenditure of this $4,000 will accomplish no object, unless it be that of attempting to defeat me at the next election in that district. I promise him that the only way he can accomplish that is to convince the people there that he is honest in his efforts to improve this harbour, and to do this he must change his policy of gr-anti g money at a time when results cannot possibly be secured so far as our harbour conditions go,

and when there is every evidence that the work is not intended to be done. Whether he defeats me or not, the protection of our public works is of more importance to me while I represent my people in this House. It cannot be said by the Government that I have not kept the facts before them year after year; nor can it be said that the Government have, made an honest effort to keep these works in good repair. I am glad that after my continued efforts I have succeeded in convincing the minister of the importance of building this western breakwater and of doing the necessary dredging, and for their .action in the matter I thank the Government. I do impress upon them, however, the extent of their failure to keep up the other breakwater; it is nothing less than a crime, and I also wish to tell the minister that I am doubtful of his sincerity with regard to the expenditure of this money.

This matter was brought to the attention of the Minister of Public Works early in the year by the hon. member, and, of course, it was impossible for him to do anything until he had the necessary amount placed in the Estimates and sary amount placed in the estimates and passed by Parliament. We could not do anything until now.
When the hon. member states that this item is probably put into the supplementary estimates on .account of an election coming on, that is hardly a fair statement, because the minister would have had these estimates before Parliament in February or March if Parliament had not adjourned. For that reason, we were not able to go on with these estimates until now. The hon. member states that we cannot go on with this work this fall. The advantage of having this amount of $18,300 in the estimates is this, that even if we cannot do anything with this work this fall, we have the money with which to go on with the work early in the spring. We can use the amoqnts in these estimates up until the beginning of April, and then we can place in next year's main estimates or supplementary estimates an amount with which to continue and complete it; $18,300 is all that the department estimate they can expend during the present fiscal year. Under the circumstances, as the Minister of Public Works took this matter up when he was making up the supplementary estimates in February last, no such charge can be made against him as that this item was inserted on account of an election coming on. It was put in because there was a
strong petition from the fishermen in the locality that the work should be done and because the officials of the department reported that it was absolutely necessary and urgent. The hon. member agrees with me now that this item is perfectly justifiable. The only claim he has is that the money cannot be expended during this fall. As I have said, this estimate lasts until the beginning of April, and, therefore, if the work cannot be done on account of storms in October or November, the work can be proceeded with next spring. The hon. member has no ground for his suspicion that this item is inserted for election purposes. It was put in, as he himself has admitted, on account of the actual necessity and urgency of the work.

I must admire the
minister's apparent candour. He tries to convince me that he did all he could do because, forsooth, he put this -item into the supplementary estimates to repair a condition that existed last year, and for the last four years, when he might, if he were sincere in his desire to repair those works, have put it into the main estimatesfl	He had a year before last February to .consider the main estimates, and he had plenty of time during his consideration of the main estimates, to consider these works. I am al6o positive that they will not make any impression upon the people whom I represent, because they are intelligent people.
There is no doubt that they are intelligent people.

The minister says that the .amounts in the supplementary estimates can be expended next year. The amounts, if they are included in the general estimates of next year, can be expended next year. It is quite apparent to my hon. friend that he cannot begin this work this fall, and the insertion of this item in the supplementary estimates is in order to hold out hopes to the people of Margaree that this work will be undertaken. What justifica-

The Government are not sincere because they will not expend the money during this winter. The majority of the people of this country are convinced that another king will reign next year and that another party will 'be in power who will expend this money, but this Government have no intention in the world to expend it. This Government did not, during the last five years, spend money that was provided by the previous Government, so that it is not very likely,, when they are inserting this item in the estimates in this slipshod manner, that they are sincere and will expend the money at this time. As I stated a few moments ago, the main estimates were made out in October last, and therefore-
The need for this expenditure existed six months, a year, two years before that.

I must say that I am not surprised at the conclusion of the minister. I would have expected no other conclusion. The sincerity in either case is questioned by me seriously. The minister, however, does not understand the conditions at Margaree. I know that. He has repeatedly stated that the ex-Minister of Public Works could not include this item in the general estimates. I cannot for the life of me understand what he has in mind. The ex-Minister of Public Works assured me a year and one-half ago that this matter was under consideration.
The elections were not decided on then.

There must be something wrong with the machinery of the Government if an item that comes to their notice in November through a report from their engineer that a public work is disappearing for want of repairs cannot be included in the estimates that are placed before the House in the following January. The matter requires some explanation from the minister.
He says the report of the engineer reached the department in November, and that it was too late then to put an item in the main estimates for this year. If that is so, I must say that the main estimates are prepared very slowly indeed. This is surely not .such a big book that it could

not be put together and printed in a few days. How is it that an urgent request made in November could not be provided for in the main estimates? The minister also promised some explanation why this long delay took plaoe. The minister has officers down there, but nothing was done, and I think it is up to him to explain who is to blame for this condition of affairs. If it is true that this breakwater could have been repaired four or five years ago at a trifling expense of $400 or $500, and we are now asked to spend $5,500 for it, simply because of some one's neglect in the department, I think the minister ought to explain who is to blame. The responsibility should be thrown on some one.

The only person I can throw it on, from the evidence I have, is engineer Bernasconi. There does not appear to be any official report earlier than November 22, 1916, but a couple of months afterwards there was a strong petition from the fishermen. I am not finding any fault with Bem-asconi. Of course, I could not censure him at all. The official report I have before me shows why the repairs were not provided for before. I do not wish to throw the blame on any one. I have no doubt at all that the hon. member brought this matter to the attention of the Minister of Public Works, but that is being done every day by members, and the minister has to consider which works are the most urgently needed. Perhaps Bernasconi did not press this as hard as the hon. member thinks he should have done. What was the date when the council approved of the estimates?
I could not say offhand.
