The estimates were all made out at the end of October by the officials of the different departments, were submitted to council and approved, and then printed.

If it is to be understood that the Government makes out its estimates in the month of October, and
that no matter how urgent a request may come in in the meantime, no further item will be included, even if the House does not meet till the middle of January, as was the case this year, a greenhorn or layman would come -to the conclusion that the Government was running its business in a very unbusinesslike way. If there is a hiatus between October and February during which no item can be added to the main estimates, the people ought to know that such is the case. On the face of it, it seems absolutely inexcusable, but there may be some technical reason to account for it.

The hon. member knows that that is not in accordance with the facts. The estimates made out in October are for expenditures to commence from the 1st of April of the following year. The hon. gentleman knows that if any urgent work is required to be done before April 1 an item can be put in the supplementary estimates. He also knows that the House meets in January of every year at the latest, and sometimes in December or November, and that supplementary estimates are always brought down shortly after Parliament meets, to take care of urgent and unforeseen expenditures. The hon. member also knows that the fact of the estimates being prepared in October, and being presented to the House in January, does not delay construction on any particular work for one minute.

I do not know anything of the kind. I repeat that it is a lamentable condition of affairs if the fishermen are to be deprived of this work because of this lapse of time, during which an item could have been put in the main estimates. The Government may be very busy, and no doubt is, but the Public Works Department is not and has not been; that department has been one of the snaps in public life in Canada since the war broke out, compared with the work required of the minister in ordinary times, because no new works on a large scale are being undertaken. There is no gainsaying that it is a very lame way of doing business if the minister knew in November by an official report that the need for this work was urgent, anl yet did not put an item in the estimates although Parliament did not meet till January. The Minister of Customs, who is Acting Minister of Public Works, said the Government had to take control into their own hands. Does he know that when a certain Bill was being discussed in committee, up to the time the Government gave notice of closure, the Conservative members had spread out their remarks to the extent of 69 columns of Hansard, while the liberals only consumed 50?
I did not know that
That is a fact.

When the hon. minister said I spoke this afternoon for the purpose of obstruction, I say his statement is not correct. I stated, as a general principle, with regard to repairs, or to public facilities of any kind, if there was to be as much delay as there has been in some cases, the *attention of the Government should be
called to it, and the system should be reformed, so that there could be quicker provision for obtaining money, and that the Government should not be compelled to wait for the sittings of Parliament, which sometimes means that a whole year will be lost. I was not referring to this particular case, but I could refer to Inverness, if I wished, or to the place the hon. gentleman comes from. The hon. gentleman from Moosejaw is a living example of why we are delayed here so long. The same thing would apply to a goodly number of members on the other side of the House. The hon. gentleman from Renfrew points to a certain debate, in which he said the members on this side of the House, being very considerably more in number than the members on the other side, took a little longer in actual debate than the members on the other side. I venture the assertion that the remarks of members on the other side have filled double as many pages of Hansard as the speeches by members supporting the Government. I would concede that, as they are the critics of the Government, it may be their right to talk more than members on the Government side. A certain number of members, particularly from the Maritime Provinces, occupy a considerable amount of the time of the House. I was going to suggest that we institute a little Parliament just for those Maritime Provinces, and I do not think it will be necessary to have a Hansard. Fifty per cent of the time of the House is occupied by members from those provinces by the sea. Many of the members from Ontario and the western provinces have privately discussed this matter and we feel that they unduly take up the time of the House. If all the members would insist upon their rights to be heard in this House to the same extent as some of those hon. gentlemen, we could not get through a session of this House in ten years, and I think some of those gentlemen who are accustomed to talking so much should stop and consider, for a little while, the other members representing constituencies in the Dominion of Canada, wTho should have something to say from time to time. We do not wish to be unreasonable



with them, and I would ask the hon. gentleman who is looking at me just now-
I am much interested.

-to look up Hansard, and see how many pages he has filled, and compare the number with the number ol pages occupied by any member on this side of the House, and I think he will not have much criticism to offer.

The hon. gentleman
from Muskoka (Mt. Wright) has given us a very timely lecture, but if it takes him three years to incubate a little bit of a speech, that is not our fault. Nature does not always produce in the same way, and, as a farmer', he knows that. Hon, members on the other side of the House are of the same class and of the same manner of production. When an important measure is .to be brought down the hon. member for Muskoka and his fellow-members have had an opportunity of seeing it perhaps a month before we see it. Therefore, if we on this side take a little longer than the .supporters of the Government, under the requirements of our constitution and form of government, there is a good reason for it. The wharf at Port Hood is an old structure commenced by the local government of Nova Scotia during 1865 and assumed by the federal Government in 1871. The original work was extended, repaired and improved by the Department of Public Works at different times but owing to its being constructed entirely with native timber, the substructure was weakened by the ravages of the teredo and it was found impossible to keep the work in proper repair. in 1911 in places where they were very much needed; the items for these were afterwards dropped from the estimates upon the assurance from the minister that they would be taken up first when new works were being considered. The minister is not
well instructed as to the prospective usefulness of this proposed wha-rf. The people of Grand river, forsooth, are going to leave their open harbour and splendid shipping accommodation on the Atlantic on the southern side of the island and pull their grain over hill and dale until they come to the Bras d'Or lakes, which they will find absolutely frozen in winter time, and they are going to camp on this new wharf at Soldier's cove until the ioe breaks up in the spring. I know the conditions down there. If the proposition were that this wharf was needed in order that the people might bring in the supplies necessary for their families, there might be some reason in it, but the proposition that the wharf is required in order that grain, etc., may be hauled away in large quantities from Soldier's cove to the markets of the world, is dreamland >so far as I know anything about the matter, and I know the locality very much better than the minister does. Some one has been imposing upon the department. This item is in exactly the same category as the item for the Ben Eoin wharf that was struck out this afternoon. There is a new candidate in that county, a great man for manipulations of this kind, who expects to run in the next election.
What is his name?
John C. Douglas.

I did not know that. I
should have left the item in, and then it would have been all right.

He finds these wonderful places. He found this place of Ben Eoin. We have heard wonderful accounts of the condition of things on the north shore of lake Superior, where men have to be tied with ropes when they work on the railroad so that they may not fall into the lake. From the description I have of this place the conditions will be very much the same; the workmen will have to be let down with cables and pulled up with cables.
Perhaps they would have to use an elevator.

Yes. This new genius who has entered into the political life of Richmond county is finding those wonderful developments that can be produced by giving him here and there a few thousand dollars to be spent on day labour in order to make promises and make votes.. The minister can have this item put through if he chooses. He can throw to the winds the honour of the gentleman whom he represents here, who has made a bargain with us that this sort of thing will not be done. I suppose he can secure a majority to smash all those regulations and all those matters of honour that have been agreed upon, if he wants to give Mr. Douglas some thousands of dollars to be spent on day labour and to allow him to promise in advance the wonderful things that are to be done. I cannot protest too vehemently against the voting and expenditure of public money under the present conditions of the country, and against conduct of this kind.

I have not heard much of the discussion this evening about this vote for Soldier's Cove wharf, but I trust the minister will agree to drop this ' item. I see the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) in his seat sitting close by the acting Minister of Public Works (Mr. Reid). I said this afternoon that the Minister of Finance, on several occasions during the past few months, solemnly promised Parliament that, during the war, no new public work would be undertaken if it were at all avoidable. Here is a proposal to spend a few thousand dollars in the construction of a wharf at a place at which, I am informed," it is absolutely unnecessary. I understand that efforts were made, during the last twenty-five years, to have this work done by the Government, but all governments have declined to proceed with it or to vote money for the purpose. It is true, there is but a small amount of money involved, but why should we vote even that small amount this year, under all the prevailing circumstances, in order to build this wharf? The minister should not require any argument to induce him to withdraw the appropriation. I should feel inclined to move that the item be dropped, but I hope the minister will follow the precedent which he set this afternoon in regard to another appropriation, and drop this one. There is no necessity for ja. wharf at this place and even if there were,

it can wait until next year. The acting minister surely would like to make a reputation for himself, while minister of this department, so as to leave a good example for the man who will later on become Minister of Public Works. Will the minister not agree to drop this item?

1 could not possibly agree to drop this small item. I do not know whether the hon. member was in the House when I read a petition from 400 families miles away from a railway, who say that they have agricultural products they want to take out from that place and no doubt they want to bring in supplies required for their own needs. This petition is signed by the people living in that locality. While theje is no doubt at all that the former Minister of Public Works said that he would strike out items and that he did strike out of the estimates items aggregating $10,000,000, he never promised, and no minister would promise, that he would not insert any items. If that petition is correct, 400 families will be accommodated by this wharf. I believe the people who signed that petition are honest people and that they would not sign it unless the work was a necessity and should be done at once. It may be true that this matter has been neglected, that the wharf has not been built before.
Wait until next year.

The hon. member this afternoon wanted every item struck out in the way of repairs to and construction of wharves for the accommodation of the people of Nova Scotia; or, in other words, he was willing that all the items in connection with Nova Scotia be struck out, while lie allowed all the items in connection with every other province to pass without a single word of protest.
No. We have not yet reached the harbour and river items of the other provinces.

The hon. member knows that we have passed all the items in the main estimates for the whole Dominion, and during the passing of all the main estimates, the hon. gentleman never raised an objection to an item in any other province, but he now says to this committee: So far as Nova Scotia is concerned, I want every single dollar of expenditure struck out of the estimates, even to the extent of $2,500 to accommodate 400 families in one district. Even though these are estimates for Nova Scotia, and I come from Ontario, I will
[Mr. A. K. Maclean. 1
stand by every item so far as Nova Scotia is concerned. It is not fair for the hon. member to take that position in regard to his own province. The former Minister of Public Works took it for granted that the people were honest in signing this petition; his officials reported that the wharf was required; and I, therefore, feel like standing by this item.

The minister is trying to make a political speech, and that will do no good here 'or any where else. I will take the responsibility for the decision I took this afternoon. I was quite willing that all these items be struck out this year. I said last evening that three or four pages of estimates of this character might very well be dropped, because I think this is a time when we should restrict our public expenditure as much as possible. Does not the minister agree with that? Now he proposes building a wharf at a place where I doubt very much if it is required, and he gives us as justification a petition. Now a petition never establishes anything. I could go to the minister's own constituency and get a petition addressed to His Excellency the Governor General, signed by hundreds of my hon. friend's own constituents praying that he be removed from office.
No, it would be the other way.
I will guarantee that the petition will be signed, and will send you to the right people.

I remember the days when my hon. friend took up considerable time of the House decrying works of this character in Nova Scotia. I have heard him repeatedly say that there was not a spot left where a wharf could be built. If there was any real necessity for this work being undertaken, the Liberal party, which was in power for fifteen years, would very likely have accomplished it. I am informed that requests for this work have been made to successive Governments by two or three people in the district, but the request was always refused by the department. If that was the policy of the department in the past, I submit that we require something more than a petition to justify this vote. Perhaps the minister will say whether any one else besides Mr. Douglas has requested this.
The petition was" signed by the people in that locality. They are the ones who have requested this work; it is not Mr. Douglas' petition at all.

I understood the minister to say that this place was only eight miles from St. Peter's. From St. Peter's to Soldier's cove, from Soldier's cove to Johnston's harbour, and from Johnston's harbour to Irish cove-that is along the southern shore of the Bras d'Or lake-is a very sparsely settled district, and Where the minister can get four 'hundred families in the eight miles between St. Peter's and Soldier's cove to sign this petition, I don't know. He talks about this place being so very remote from a railway. As a matter of fact, there is a railway only eight miles from St. Peter's, and that road connects with the Intercolonial. I represent a county which at its extreme northern end is 110 miles from a railway. Three-fourths of my county is more than forty miles from a railway. But there is no use my talking to the Minister ,of Railways about that, for he won't do anything for me. Then a little below this place is Johnston's harbour, where the boat we were speaking of calls. There is not the slightest reason for this item at all, except to put $2,500 in the hands of the minister's political friends to spend on timber and sticks, and they will promise to give fellows a day's work when the election comes on; that is all this vote is for. The county of Richmond was represented by Liberals practically for the whole fifteen years Sir Wilfrid Laurier was in power, and if there was any necessity for this work being undertaken the wharf would have been built in our time. One was built at Irish cove, and another at Johnston's harbour, and another at St. Peter's. The minister is well aware of conditions in his own part of the country, where there are farms running down to the lakes, and he knows that if there is a public wharf every eight miles or so the people are doing pretty well. It is only eight miles between Johnston's harbour and this place, and another eight miles to the canal, where there is a wharf. There is no justification whatever for the minister pressing this item through, even if we did not have the promise of the late Minister of Public Works that no new undertakings would be entered upon until financial conditions changed, and I feel confident that if that hon. gentleman (Mr. Rogers) were still in charge of the department he would have kept his word and these new items would not have been put through.

The minister does not reply, so it is pretty hard to tell what he intends to do about this matter. He has
referred to a petition that was sent to him', but has made no reference to the report of the engineer. If there is any doubt as to the facts the minister should be able to find out the truth in the report of the engineer. The minister knows the usual way of dealing with a petition when it comes to the department. It is referred to the district engineer, who examines into the facts and makes a report to the minister, and I venture to say that it very often turns out that the report of the engineer is very different from the statements made in the petition. The minister has not said very much about the report of his engineer on this undertaking. My hon. friend from North ^Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) has pointed out that the district is pretty well accommodated already, and that this wharf will be so far away from the people the minister says it is intended to serve that they will use other wharves.
In explaining to the people I represent why .the various items for works along the coast were struck out of the estimates, I gave the promise of the late Minister of Public Works that whenever the Government began to construct new works those items that were struck out would be gone on with first. Does the promise of the late Minister of Public Works go for nothing? Is the present Minister of Public Works not going to observe it? If new wharves are to be constructed I want to put in a claim for the wharf that was dropped in my constituency, and which accommodates three villages and a large district along the coast. I urge the minister to restore the item for a wharf at Cole harbour, because from what I know of both localities this work is much more important than the other. I should like a statement from the minister as to whether or not he intends to disregard the pledge that was given the House by the late Minister of Public Works.

I should like to keep this item in, but in view of the discussion I will take this matter up with my officials and investigate it further. If we pass the item, we should then be prepared to go bn with the work, if inquiry justifies it. .
Will the minister let the item stand in the meantime?

It is only a small item and I think we had better put it through. I don't think my hon. friend should ask me to let it stand. I may have to get a report from the engineer in that locality, and the hon. gentleman knows that, at this late

hour, of the session, it would be impossible to get the report in time. I will ask the deputy to look into the matter thoroughly. After this discussion, they will not pro. ceed with the work, and I am not going to push it. It is not the desire of the Government to expend any money where it is not really necessary. 'It might possibly be that they have been, wrongly informed, but the discussion has brought .the matter very forcibly before the department, and before I undertake the expenditure, I will take the matter up with the engineer and other members of the staff, and go into it thoroughly. I would not like to strike the item out and ascertain later, on investigation, that, in the opinion of the department, i.t should have been passed.

The late Minister of
Public Works is sitting behind the hon. gentleman just now, and can speak in regard to the pledge given to the members when other items were struck out. If this item is to be struck out, what are you going to do about the Cole harbour item, which has been dropped?

The only thing I could do
would be to bring down another estimate, but we are not going to present any more estimates, so that I cannot do .anything in connection with that item this session. We have brought all the items we intend to submit this session.

If we are to abandon the position which the minister helped us to take, when he asked us to hold back and say nothing, as there was a strong reason for not going on with construction. What about the next item?
Sydney river-wharf at Perry Lewis, $3,300
What are we to say about .the Sydney river item, if we let the Soldier's cove item go through?

The discussion brings the
matter to the attention of the department, and if it is found they are not absolutely required the items will stand; but I do not think it is fair to ask us to strike out the items altogether.
We should all be treated alike.
These repairs are provided for in every constituency.

The hon. gentleman is wrong in saying that we are criticising the items for repairs. They are absolutely necessary, and I have no fault to find with
rMr. J. D. Reid.]
them. Repairs have been much neglected, but repairs and new items are quite different.

I was not finding fault with the hon. gentleman in regard to his criticism of items for repairs, but I wish to impress upon him that, so far as repairs and a few little items for new wharves are concerned, these are distributed in the constituencies of members on both sides of the House.

The hon. minister provides for three new wharves in the same riding. The item for Ben Eoin wharf is dropped. Soldier's cove is another new item, and the wharf on Sydney river is a third item. There may be more. Why should this constituency be singled out from the others? So far as I know, there is nothing else new in the province.
My hon. friend says these are all in one riding. Sydney river is in Cape Breton county, and Soldier's cove is in Richmond county.
For the purpose of the next election, they are in the same constituency.
I do not know.
South Cape Breton and Richmond are the same riding.
They are like Leeds and Broekville. [DOT]

Leeds and
Broekville are a combination of two constituencies-a double-barreled constituency.

We have the same agency presenting these three items. The gentleman who is to be the candidate for South Cape Breton and Richmond is bringing pressure to bear on the department for these new items. It is not fair to the rest of us, and I am sure there should be some place where we can get a decent show from the Government. The older members, such as the hon. member from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) myself, and others, had items in the estimates in 1912, and they went through while this Government was in power, and when they dropped them they gave us the explanation that the revenue had dropped, and later that the war was on, and, we were to let the items stand. A new candidate comes in among us, and he gets at least three new items in his riding, for the construction of brand-new works, and our old works are to be dropped and nothing to be done about them. I submit it is absolutely unfair, and not the kind of treatment
SEPiTEMBER 4, 1917
that should be meted out to gentlemen who are willing to take the hon. minister's word lor it, and keep absolutely quiet. I wrote to my constituents, saying that, by reason of the falling off of revenue and other great demands on the treasury of the country, these works could not be proceeded with. Now we have a different condition of things entirely. The minister has no reports from his engineers on this matter, and that is another reason why it should be allowed to stand. It was the custom, when I had anything to do with works of this kind, when petitions were presented and letters forwarded, to send these petitions and letters to the engineer, and he would report, and the decision would depend upon his report. Why was this matter not sent to Mr. Bernasconi for report? But we have nothing but this petition, which is of the most absurd character. It says that people from Grand river have to come over thirty miles to this place for a decent wharf. The same is true in regard to Loch Lcmond and other places. It accommodates a few people at Soldier's cove, but accommodates nobody else. I should like to have the minister send that petition to his engineer at North Sydney, and have a report, and if that report is favourable I will not say one word against it; but until he has something tangible I will oppose it.
What does the minister say to that proposal?

I will have the petition sent back again to the engineer. I will get his report as to the necessity of this wharf before we proceed with the work. I shall have the deputy minister take up these three items, and unless, upon investigation, we find them to be urgent we will not proceed with them. No one wants to spend money if it is not necessary. But the former Minister of Public Works had a very strong petition asking for this wharf and I feel I should not be justified in striking the item out at this late stage of the session, when I should not have an opportunity to have it reinstated. Therefore, I will have to ask the committee to allow the item to stand in the Estimates on the understanding that we will make a thorough investigation before proceeding with the work.

The Minister of Finance has been advertising for people of ordinary means to buy war certificates. Suppose he put an advertisement in a paper in Sydney asking for a number of men and women to
buy $100 certificates in order to spend the money on these three new works, do you think he would get eighty applications? It is going to take eighty of these $100 certificates to build these three new works, which the men living in that vicinity say are not needed. The Minister of Finance is asking us to put forth every effort to secure money by the thousands, and down to a hundred and to five and ten dollars. At such a time as this, does the hon. Acting Minister of Public Works think it is fair, in view of the fact that men coming from these constituencies protest that the expenditure is not needed, that the Government should take eighty of these $100 certificates and put them into new work?
The Minister of Finance, the . Minister of Agriculture, and other members of this House have been urging the people to produce more.
And to save.

And to save. We have been urging the people to raise more agricultural products. They say: We are producing more, but we require better transportation. Then, having asked them to produce more, shall we refuse to spend $2,500?
It is $8,000 for the three items.

Here is one item with regard to which 400 families represent to us that they have taken the advice of the Minister of Finance and produced more. If they have produced $300,000 more in agricultural products surely we can spend $2,500 to get the products out. All over this country we are extending railway sidings and helping people, when they do produce, to get their products out. With this expenditure of $2,500-
Eight thousand dollars for the three items.
Yes, but the larger expenditure accommodates more families.

It is not the amount
particularly, although these small amounts combined form a very large sum. The members of this -House who are responsible to these people tell the minister that the petition is not well founded and that several of the localities mentioned in the petition are nearer by eight miles to a wharf already constructed than they are to this point. Many of those who, the minister says will be accommodated will have to pass one wharf and some of them two. Some of

them will have to leave a wharf on the Atlantic coast and go 25 miles back to the Bras d'Or lakes. Surely a member of Parliament living in the vicinity knows what he is talking about. If I were the minister and. a member for the constituency said: " Leave it out," I would leave it out so quickly that it would surprise him. But the fact is that it is a man not in this House who is urging this and you have three new items in one constituency amounting to $8,000 which the men- representing that constituency in this House say are not needed. Surely the minister has every reason to strike them out, if it be not that in the political sense they are going to help somebody. In these times we have to drop that kind of thing.

The hon. member (Mr. Graham) suggests that the members representing the constituency have said that it is not a necessary work. If my memory serves me, the member representing that constituency said that every work provided for in the constituency was an absolute necessity. Even the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) did not say that this was not necessary; he said that these items were necessary. Is it fair for the hon. member (Mr. Graham) to ask me to strike out this item because members in other constituencies say it is not necessary? The hon. member is hardly fair when he says that members residing in the constituency have asked me to strike it out,
Here is a member (Mr. McKenzie) who is right adjoining and he knows all about it.
But that is another constituency. The member representing the constituency said that every item was a necessity.

The mill to which they would send the grain is in my constituency and I am sure that I would be willing to draw grist to my own mill. If there was any grain at Johnston's harbour or at Soldier's cove across the lake,' that would come out by this wharf, it would have to come to this provincial mill in n v constituency and I	would be
very sorry to say a word against it. There are wharves at Irish cove, Johnston's harbour and St. Peter's, and I will give the minister $5 for every bushel of grain that any one ever sold at any one of these wharves that were built fifteen or twenty years ago. The statement in the

petition is absolutely false although the minister may believe it in preference to my word if he likes.

It is quite clear that the minister is not going to regard the promise made by his predecessor. He is apparently willing to treat it as a " scrap of paper." The main question before the committee is:	Are we going to keep faith with the
members of this House when a promise of that kind is made?
I have put up with items for my constituency being struck out, on the ground that every dollar was required for other purposes. I submitted to the proposal of the late minister that these matters should lie over, with the distinct understanding that when new construction was undertaken they would have precedence of all other claims. The minister has not dealt with that point. He says this is a small item. But it is not small when you consider the promise made to the House. There is no question that promise was made; the minister does not deny it. If his only reason is that this will help some one politically, that is a very poor reason indeed at a time like this. This Government has the reputation of being very partisan, and they need to do something drastic in order to convince people that they are not thinking all the time about keeping themselves in power, and that they have some regard for the public interest. I put it to the minister that he ought to do this for the reputation of the department and for the reputation of the retiring minister, who gave us that pledge. Is he or is he not going to keep that promise? There are other similar items in the other provinces. The minister said that we had passed one already, but the fact that we passed one without any one noticing it is no reason why we should pass these items. If he can justify these items, there is no reason why he should not build a new wharf in every constituency where a Conservative candidate asks him to do so.

I do not think I can add anything to what I have said. There is no danger of any more wharfs or other work being proceeded with than are provided for in the estimates. I do not think the exminister promised not to go on with any new work, as that would prevent his acting in cases of urgency. Nor do I think it would !be fair to strike this out when the member for the constituency has agreed with the late Minister of Public Works and has said that every one of these works is necessary.

This is not in Mr. Carroll's constituency now, although it will be for the election for which this vote is intended. If the minister will consult his files ,he will find that no one asked for this except Mr. Douglas, who is not a member but will be a candidate in this election. Have we the promise of the minister that he will obtain a report from the engineer at North Sydney and submit it to the House before proceeding with this work:

I shall tell the deputy minister now to write to the engineer instructing him to investigate and see if the work is urgently required, and we will act on the report of the engineer in that district.
South Side (Donald's Head) Cape Sable Island-breakwater extension, $1,800.

This is asked for by Engineer Lock. It is for an extension 40 feet long, 30 feet wide and 17 feet high to the outer end of the breakwater. It ie required to enable coasting steamers to call at all times of tide.
Sydney river-wharf at Perry Lewis, $3,300.
This is another stormy petrel, and if the minister gets it through to-night it will be as much as 1 can promise him. This is in the city of Sydney.
This is for a wharf at Perry Lewis.

This is practically in
the city of Sydney. There is a Government wharf in the city of Sydney already. The shore of the harbour is lined 9 p.in. with wharves. Why in the name of anything that is sensible are we going to put another Government wharf in the city of Sydney? The thing is most absurd.

The report I have says that Assistant Engineer MeKeen says that Sydney river is a settlement on the southern arm of Sydney harbour, at the mouth .of Sydney river. The site is three miles from the city of Sydney, about 500 feet below Gibbons' bridge. The settlement is the centre of a flourishing district and there are quite a number of summer cottages owned . and occupied in summer by Sydney residents. The residents applied for the construction of a wharf so that steamers plying on Sydney harbour might be induced to call for passengers and farm products, etc. Then it would also be used by picnic parties. During the past years steamers carrying parties were compelled to carry a scow or scows and transfer their passengers at high tide.

Three miles from Sydney ! I hope there is somebody here who knows Sydney. That place is not more than a quarter of a mile from the city limits, if it is not within them. The city runs about two miles along the water front and here we have a representation that this is three miles from Sydney. There is only one solitary merchant in that vicinity and you are going to give him a wharf. The Intercolonial passes right by his door and there is a siding at Gibbons' bridge, 500 feet away. No boats .pass this point, as Gibbon's bridge is the end of the harbour. This man Lewis is doing a little business up there, and if the Government build him a wharf they will find that every merchant in the city will want one also. They have just as much right to it as Perry Lewis has.

The only information I have in regard to the matter is that which has been placed at my disposal by the department. In view of the statement that has been made by the hon. member, we will not proceed with the work unless, after investigating the matter, we find that the work is absolutely necessary. In view of the representations made by the department with respect to the alleged necessity for the wharf, I cannot understand how the conditions can be as the hon. member states.

If the minister is going to make inquiry into the matter, he ought to inquire what steamers are to call at that wharf. The bridge across the river 500 feet further up is the end of navigation on Sydney harbour. The main post road bridge, or Gibbons bridge, and the railway bridge cross there side by side. There is no draw on the railway bridge, and I do not think there is any on Gibbons' bridge. The minister may be under the impression that quite a number of steamers pass up and down there and call at that wharf. If steamers do call, what are they going to call for? For passengers? Where are the passengers to come from? There is only one merchant there; I suppose we are going to build a wharf for him. The Intercolonial passes at his door; there is a small station at the end of Gibbon's bridge, 500 feet away. Moreover, there is a Government wharf in the city. The member for Lunenburg (Mr. D. Stewart) calls out "carried." If items affecting the county of Lunenburg were under consideration, l should have very little to say, but when the hon. member calls "carried" at this rime he does not know what he is talking

about; he does not know anything about this vote. If he is here as the speqial agent of John C. Douglas, I can understand why he is parroting the word "carried" every time an argument is advanced from this side of the House.

I was not aware that I had opened my mouth, much less said anything. On a previous occasion the hon. member accused me of interrupting him; I can assure him that I was not conscious of having interrupted him to-night. I know very little about this matter. I do know something of the locality affected by this vote, but nothing that would be of any value to the minister or to the committee. I rise merely to correct the assertion of the hon. gentleman that I interrupted him, for I had no intention of doing that.

I did not say that the hon. gentleman was interrupting me; nor did I regard the remark as an interruption. But he is continually crying out "carried" when I am trying to explain to the minister the conditions in my own constituency, with which I am familiar. I do not regard it as courteous for an hon. member who knows nothing about the situation to be continually crying out "carried."

I did not even use the word "carried." I had not opened my mouth to speak-I may have opened my mouth, but not to speak. I was not interfering with the discussion, for the reason, as the hon. gentleman says, that I know very little about the matter under consideration.

The minister has not answered the contention that this place has already sufficient accommodation. He has struck out several items in respect of works on the Atlantic coast of Nova Scotia, where there is no accommodation-places situated fifty miles from a railway, where a public wharf would afford, the people their only facility for the shipment of fish, the landing of coal, etc. He appears to be willing, at the instance of the Conservative candidate, to build a wharf at a place which is close to a railway station and which has ample accommodation-a place occupied by only one merchant. I should like him to justify that if he can.

The hon. gentleman, who lives in the constituency, knows the locality better than I do. Evidently the former Minister of Public Works, when he made out these estimates, considered, in view of the information before him, that this work 
was necessary. I feel, therefore, that rather than strike this item out we should take the matter up again with the officials at Sydney. If the statements made by the member for North Cape Breton are in accordance with the facts, we shall not go ahead with the wharf. It would be absurd to build a wharf at a place where only one man lives and where there is practically no freight. I have instructed the deputy minister to take this matter up with the engineer down there and to refer him to the statements of the member for that district. Unless he can show that the statements made are not in accordance with the facts, I would not proceed with the work.
Is it correct to say that Mr. John C. Douglas asked for this wharf?
Mr. John C. Douglas has asked for work in that constituency. But, besides Mr. Douglas, other persons have made application; petitions have come in from other sources.
I do not care anything about other petitions; who asked for this work?
Supposing it was Mr. Douglas-
Who is Mr. Douglas?
He is a member of the provincial legislature; he represents the constituency in question.
Is he a Tory?

He certainly is, so far as I know, but the fact of his being a Tory is no reason why he should not look after the interests of the constituency he represents. He is a member of the local legislature. I think, therefore, he is perfectly justified in asking for anything he thinks is absolutely required. His constituents would no doubt intercede with him in his capacity as their member and endeavour to. have their requirements brought before the proper department at Ottawa.
Is Mr. Douglas a candidate for Parliament?
He is a member of the local legislature for that constituency and has been for many years.
Is he a candidate for the Federal Parliament?
I live in Ontario, and I know only the candidates in that province. I cannot say anything as to the candidates in Nova Scotia.
Will the minister consult the sitting member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) in regard to this expenditure?
I cannot say whom the exMinister of Public Works consulted. I am consulting the hon. member for the constituency now and will deal with the matter afterwards.
It is rather late now.

This is a protection for the new wharves that have been built at St. John. It is claimed that this protection is an urgent necessity on account of the flow of water around the new wharves. The Secretary of the St. John Board of Trade writes as follows under date March 31:
The experiences of the past winter have so strongly emphasized the necessity tor the extension of the Negrotown breakwater to Partridge Island that the council of the St. John Board of Trade has directed me to ask you whether it is the intention of your department to proceed with this work during the coming spring and summer, so that it may be ready for next winter. Not only are the new government piers endangered by the undertow which sweeps through the west channel at times, but shipping at these and other piers has been imperilled and in some instances damage has resulted.

There is some comfort
in that statement. I am very glad indeed that the gang in St. John, who have been manipulating the thing for the last three or four years, won't get their fingers in the pie this time. But while it may be an Ontario firm by name, I think you will find the patronage committee in St. John will

be in it just the same. You cannot eliminate them as long as this Government continues to be run as it is. But that is not the point I am making. But why should the minister expend this enormous amount just now when an election is coming on? Down in New Brunswick whenever an election is coming on friends of my hon. friend always get busy. Let me give him a little illustration. An election was brought on last February and a contract was made to build a railroad. Two days after that Tennant cashed the cheque, and paid $20,000 to Mr. Thomas Bell, another member of the patronage committee, and a director of the St. John Standard, just a little ring that manipulates things in St. John
The Standard Railway?

They were very open about it, and paid the money over to the patronage committee, and distributed it around. Knowing as I

do what is going on in St. John, and in New Brunswick generally, and knowing the barefaced way in which they take money voted for public purposes, I cannot view this vote with anything but suspicion, based upon almost actual knowledge that an election was coming on. I do not know what the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) may say, and do not care very much, nor do I care what the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries may say, but I protest against this Government entering into a quarter million dollars expenditure for election purposes in St, John under these conditions. No man need tell me it is a prime necessity to have the breakwater extended. I admit that the extension would improve the harbour of St. John. In time it should be extended. The present channel between the breakwater and Partridge island should be filled in, and it would be a great benefit to shipping; hut they can handle the shipping there just as well next year as they have done for the past five years, and last year there was more tonnage out of St. John, by twenty-five or fifty per cent, than ever handled before. doubt they require all the berths they have got, and probably more, and if my hon, friend were building wharves, I would not say anything about it, because, under present conditions, with the enormous amount of traffic going from this country across the water, and with the necessity of making the harbour of St. John as convenient as possible, and rendering all the necessary aid to the exportation of our products, and it being the terminus of the Canadian Pacific railway on the Atlantic coast, it is all right to build wharves. But when they commence to talk about the breakwater, which has been discussed since I was a boy-I can hardly remember a time when they did not talk about extending Negro Head breakwater-it looks to me so much like election campaign matter that I cannot help voting against it. The minister should consider carefully before rushing the country into an expenditure of a million dollars-it may be two million dollars; they admit a quarter of a million for a starter. I protest against it, and I believe the vote should be dropped.

Before deciding the motion of my hon. friend and before passing the vote, it would be only right that some information should be given. There is no doubt that for many years there has been
an urgent demand from some quarters for the extension to Partridge island. When I was minister I had plans prepared, after consultation with those acquainted with the harbour which included two things-building the breakwater from Partridge island eastward, and filling up the gaps between the present breakwater and Partridge island. There was quite a difference of opinion at that time as to whether it was desirable to extend the breakwater or not, because the space between the breakwater and the island was used quite largely by small vessels coming into the harbour, and there was also the objection that if the breakwater were extended, and that channel filled in, the result might be to cause a current from the harbour directly outward to the Bay of Fundy; but I think, upon the whole, the people who are best qualified to judge are of the opinion that it would be desirable that the breakwater should be extended and this gap filled in. My own judgment is that the work of building the breakwater from the island is equally important, if not more important, and of course would cost very much less than I understand this work is going to cost. But there is nothing that I can say which would induce the minister to make provision for the immediate construction of the breakwater from the island eastward. The vote could not be changed to accomplish that, and, therefore, the question is, whether or not it is desirable to go on with the work. There is no doubt the condition of affairs in the harbour of St. John has been greatly changed by the dredging out of a very large area on the western side of the harbour, and I believe it is true that in times of storm there is considerable danger to shipping on the west side which it is thought would be obviated if the gaps were filled in. Would the minister tell me/ what is	the difference between

made by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) and the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) to-night, I would ask that the item stand, so that I may have an opportunity of looking over the tenders and coming to some decision as to what action the department will take. particularly, but it would seem to me that under ordinary conditions that would be a benefit to the harbour. I do hope the Maritime Dredging company will not have any hand in this. If the minister does not know about the Maritime Dredging company, I might explain that it took a big part in the elections of 1911. In the Public Accounts Committee we spent three weeks talking about the Maritime Dredging company and its enormous profits. About ten days after the election I was in St. John and I saw all this crowd that had been running things go into a room in the Royal hotel and they simply took over the Maritime Dredging company and changed it from a Liberal organization to a Tory organization. Of all the raw deals that this Government has been the victim of since 1911, none could exceed the deals that have been put over by the Maritime Dredging company. There is nothing that they have not had a hand in around the city of St. John. They bought out the plant and contracts of the old Maritime Dredging company. The Conservative members of this House, and even my hon. friend the present minister, went around talking themselves red in the face before the elections about the iniquitous prices that were paid to the Maritime Dredging company, but when the new organization took charge they went right on and paid the same prices and extended their contracts; no tenders called for. There was nothing going on in St. John that they did not take a hand in for the purpose of making money. They even built wharves. And such a mess as they made of it! They had a contract to build a line of wharves and they built berth No. 17. They built a concrete wharf in the harbour of St. John, You could stand at one end and look down the line, 700 or 800 feet long, and it looked just like the waves of the sea, going three or four feet in and out. It wa6 all level at the start, but it had no foundation and it went up and down. I was down there about a year ago and I 339
went out on the wharf. They were taking hundreds of thousands of yards of spoil from Courtenay bay, for the dredging of which certain people had been paid a large price, and they were dumping this spoil in the middle of the wharf. When they got a certain amount of spoil in the middle of the v/harf the walls began to bulge out. Then they put some hawsers across, reminding me of the way in which a farmer fastens his sled stakes with hay wire. But the "hay wire" did not hold. Yet they paid the Maritime Dredging company for putting this stuff in. If there is anything that is vicious in connection with the Public Works Department it is its connection with the Maritime Dredging company and with this whole St. John business. There never were any wharves needed worse in the whole British Empire during the last two or three years than these wharves have been. Hundreds of thousands and millions of dollars have been spent in order that this crowd in St. John might make money, and any man who knows anything about the record of this company gets a little suspicious about any further work being done in the harbour of St. John. If the minister ever decides to let this work, I suggest to him that no St. John men be connected with it, especially the St. John men who were up here in the last eight or ten days. Ontario-Bruce Mines-dredging, $21,000.

This amount is required for the dredging of a basin in front of the Bruce Mines Trap Rock Company's wharf, to permit vessels to use the wharf, which, under existing conditions it is very difficult to do. The estimated cost is as follows: 6,500 cubic yards, class A, at $3, $19,500;
5,000	cubic yards, class B, at 30 cents, $1,500.
Do other vessels stop there, besides the Bruce Mines vessels? The hon. gentleman referred to a certain company's wharf?
The work is in front of the company's wharf, and all vessels stop at this wharf, so the deputy minister tells me.
Who has the contract?

It is not under contract yet.
Burlington! channel-In full and final settlement of all claims of D, G. Stewart in connection with his contract for construction of revetment wall, $10,441.
When was that contract completed?

This amount is required to pay Mr. D. G. Stewart in full of claims in connection with the construction of a revetment wall at Burlington, as authorized by Order in Council of 15th May, 1917. On August 3rd, 1915, while the work was in progress, an unusually violent storm occurred, the gale reaching a velocity of 48 miles an hour. Extensive damage was done to the revetment wall. The contractor filed a claim with the Department of Public Works to be paid the sum of $18,377.43, in addition to what was paid to him under the contract. The chief engineer gives each item in this memorandum. This claim may be summarized as follows:
1.	Making good damage done by tbe storm of August 3, 1915. This amount includes $1,064.21 for injuries to a derrick and scow... $14,77S.18
2.	Change in location of cross cribs
at openings, and concrete work. .	1,326.25
3.	Additional cost for placing talus stone in the year 1916, 2,273
cubic yards at $1 a cubic yard. ..	2,273.00
The auditor of the Chief Engineer's branch, after a careful examination of the contractors' books, pay-sheets, accounts, etc., covering repairs made to the damaged portion of the work, found that the total cost to the contractor for making good the damage caused by the storm amounts to $9,896.16.

Would not the terms of the contract made originally include everything of that kind? When the contractor tendered for this work, did he not, ae a matter of fact, take all the chances himself as to what condition should arise? It is customary where work is being done in a dangerous place for a price to be fixed accordingly, and the contractor takes all the risks of what may ensue.

This was a most violent
storm. The deputy tells me that where a contractor has met with a very heavy loss on account of serious storms, such as sometimes occur, the department have not taken advantage of the terms of the contract, and after they have gone into the matter thoroughly, they have paid claims of this kind.

If, for example, down on the Atlantic coast, the Railway Department would do this, it would be in trouble all the time, because the -work at times is very difficult on account of the storms that may arise. Contractors invariably figure on the situation, and the conditions that are likely to arise, when they .make their tender. I understand a man could put in a lower tender if he did not take into account this kind of thing, if he were sure the department would come to his rescue in case a storm destroyed his plant. I think a claim of that nature has been standing for many years in the Department of Railways and

Canals, in reference to something that occurred along the coast of one of the Great I akes, 'but the department contended that the contractor had taken all the risk himself, and tha other contractors had tendered higher, hut that he had received it on account of his lower tender, and that when he came to add the amount of his damage to the amount of his tender, his tender would be really higher than, the tender which had been rejected.

The deputy tells me it was an exceptional thing. Mr. D. G. Stewart, of Ottawa, was the contractor, and I understand that where a storm of very unusual violence destroys the contractor's work and causes an enormous amount of damage, so that the contractor does not make anything out of his contract, the department have paid. And so they have decided to pay this claim.
Collingwood - harbour Improvements- (revote, $72,000), $75,000.

Is that a continuation
of the work?

The district engineer recommends the following improvements:
(a)	The construction of a wharf 800 x 55, having cribwork substructure and concrete superstructure, and the dredging of a slip and turning basin at Beech street, estimated cost $196,016.86.
(b)	The reconstruction in concrete of the superstructure of the west breakwater, 700 x 22, and of the east breakwater, 1,815 x 24, $200,615.
It is estimated we would spend about $72,000 of that this year. This work has not been commenced.

It was voted last year,
and why was it not commenced?
Mr. CURRIE-: It was voted for an elevator.
Why did they not spend it last year?

Because they had not started the elevator.
Port Dover-repairs to piers-revote, $6,000.
Why were those piers not fixed last year?

In a. memolandum dated 6th June, 1917, the chief engineer states that tha cost of the necessary repairs will be from $2,500 to $6,000, and that the exact amount cannot he estimated until such time as the repairs are actually commenced. Acting district engineer Stevens in a report dated May 5th, 1917, states as follows:

The entrance piers to Port Dover are in a very dilapidated condition. If these piers are not to be rebuilt during the present fiscal year, it will be necessary to provide money for patching and renewing portions of the superstructure of both the east and west piers.
Port Hope-harbour improvements, $13,500.
What is the explanation of that item ?

It is for the renewal of
100 lineal feet of the revetment wall on the west side of the harbour in front of the Brandon Shell Company's factory at $55 per foot, $5,500.
Has this repair anything to do with that shell factory? [DOT]
No.

The company has gone
out of business. I understand the ferry which carries coal across the lake lands at Cobourg, and not at Port Hope.
Yes.

Some person told me
that the ferry landed at Cobourg rather than at Port Hope, on account of the inefficiency of the harbour and poor landing at Port Hope.

The Grand Trunk have their own landing at Cobourg. They have been there for years, and they never really started at Port Hope. Port Hope people were fighting for the traffic but they did not get it.
Manitoba-Little Pembina river-diversion into Pelican lake, $12,500.
What is the explanation?

This amount is asked for by Acting District Engineer Taylor for the construction of a small diversion dam in the Little Pembina river and the excavation of a channel with stop-log control from the Pembina river to Pelican lake, a distance of 4,500 feet.
Selkirk - shipyard, including arrears of rental and interest thereon, $7,200.
What is the explanation?

This amount of $7,200 is required to pay for the purchase of land which is being used as a ship yard by this department at Selkirk and is made up as follows:
Purchase of land from Mr. T. A. Burrows as per Order in Council of June 21, 1909, $5,000; rental for same:	12 yearly instalments of $140 with interest at 5 per ' cent (simple), $2,142-$7,14-2.

What kind of boats do
they build there?
This is where we lay up our dredge.
Does the minister pretend to tell us that the department let the rental run for twelve years and now proposes to pay interest on irt?	[DOT]>-

This land was purchased by Order in Council in 1909. Mr. Burrows could not give title and that is the reason why payment is delayed. They had to pay him rent until he gave title. If they had paid for the cost of the land there would not have been interest upon it. The amount of $2,142 is less than the interest would have been on the money for that time.
Why could not the rent have been paid every year?

They were waiting for the '
title.
They did not need any title to pay the rent.
No, but they purchased the land and instead of settling for the interest they gave him a rental.
They did not give it to him; they promised it.

He was entitled to the
money by that Order in Council 1909.

I am pointing out the
slipshod way of doing business.

The deputy minister tells me it was Mr. Burrows' fault. He could not produce the title until this time. Instead of paying interest they paid him a rental.
British Columbia-Fraser river-dredging in North Arm, $100,000.
- This is a big item.

This dredging will be 150 feet wide, carrying a depth of 10 feet at low water from the end of the present Channel at Iona island to the city of New Westminster. The work is asked for in a resolution passed at a joint meeting of the South Vancouver Board of Trade and Municipal Council on April 16, 1917, and in a letter, dated May 9, 1917, from the corporation of the district of Burnaby. The object of this dredging is to give a channel 10 feet deep at low tide from Iona island to the east boundary of Burnaby to serve the industries that are situated on the north arm of the Fraser river.

In what way is this different from the item in connection with St. John harbour that was held up a while
ago? No doubt, in ordinary times it might be of some benefit to industry in that province, but it does seem to be an inopportune time to spend nearly a quarter of a million dollars on dredging in the north arm. There is also the next item on "improvements and repairs." I do not know anything about the location and therefore I cannot discuss it intelligently, but it is going into a pretty big expenditure and it seems to be a new work. Unless there i3 some explanation this item should stand.
It is a new work. New Westminster is growing very fast and it appears this work is necessary. However, the item is large and perhaps I had better let it stand until I get further information.

This is not a new work. This is a continuation of a work commenced about four years ago and which was finished about three months ago. One contract was let for the larger part of the dredging necessary the channel being part of the entrance to the north arm. This is for a continuation of the large contract amounting to $850,000 and running up towards the city of New Westminster. The urgency which caused the board of trade and council of the two municipalities concerned to pass the resolutions referred to arose from the letting of a contract for the building of ships for the Imperial Munitions Board to a yard in South Vancouver. They realized that when they launched these ships they would not be sure of being able to float them unless the dredging under contemplation by the department were proceeded with. That is the reason why these two bodies acted together and urged on the Government the continuation of the work that has been going oil for three years past.

Do I understand the
hon. member to say that they are building ships at Vancouver, and that they require dredging at New Westminster, 14 or 15 miles away, to enable them to launch those ships?
It is not at New Westminster. The location of the shipyard is at South Vancouver, four miles from the end of the present dredging, and about ten miles below New Westminster.
Why all this dredging if it is below the city of New Westminster?

There are two channels in the Fraser river between the mouth and New Westminster. The dredging of the north arm was undertaken a few years

ago because that is the channel most commonly used by the traffic between the west coast of British Columbia and Fraser river points, the distance through the north arm being from 8 to 12 miles, according to the draught of the vessel, shorter than through the main channel into the Fraser river. Another reason is that the main river is so *much exposed to storms that very serious loss occurs in the towing of booms of logs that are used in the mills on the Fraser river. Besides the reasons connected with the towing of logs, the district along the north arm of the Fraser is regarded as the main industrial location for what is known as Greater Vancouver, being away from the congestion of Vancouver city and offering very unusual facilities for industrial enterprises of all kinds. They already have two lines of railway along the shore line there hut for the want of proper connection at all stages of the tide there has been great reluctance to locate industrial establishments there unless the owners of these establishments were assured of the dredging. The city of New Westminster, about fourteen years ago, obtained the services of the eminent engineer, Le Baron, who made very complete plans showing how the river might be developed. It is on these Le Baron plans that this Government plan has been prepared. As a matter of fact, the work was promised by the late Government but only put into effect since the last general election. It is part of a well designed and well considered plan made by Engineer Le Baron so long ago as 1904, and has been part of the fixed policy of the two Governments from that time until the present.
My hon. friend's explanation does not sound as well in Parliament as, perhaps, it would in his newspaper.

So keenly interested are the people of the district in this matter that, on a recent occasion, when the candidate of the hon. gentleman's' party for the district bordering on the north arm returned to that district from Ottawa, he announced in Vancouver, as one of the triumphs of his visit to Ottawa, that he had called at the Public Works Department and there secured an appropriation of $100,000 for this dredging, which was so necessary to his constituency.
What is the candidate's name?
C. E. Macdonald.
He is on the food controller's staff?
He says so.

My hon. friend has given another reason why this should not go through, because if a Grit politician can come down to Ottawa and pull off a stunt like this it seems to me the matter is open to very grave suspicion. I have no doubt that ultimately this work ought to be done. Would the hon. member state as a fact that vessels could not be launched and taken to the Fraser river without this dredging? We get suspicious sometimes when we hear these loyal reasons given for certain things. I do not think the hon. member would go so far as to say that the Imperial Munitions Board has been foolish enough to let a contract for the building of a ship in a yard from which it cannot be taken to deep water.

I said that was the occasion of the resolutions of the two councils mentioned by the minister. The firm in question was Harrison & Lamont. In addition to moving the councils, they sent me a very urgent telegram. I do not know either of these gentlemen, but as one of the two members interested, my district being on one side of the channel and Vancouver on the other, they urged me to do what I could for this dredging.
(Mr. CARVELL: No doubt hon. members supporting the Government have received urgent requests from all over Canada, and quite proper ones. I am not finding any fault with the expenditure of public money on public works, but I do not think I have to go over again the very very serious financial problems we are facing in Canada at the present time. If I can believe what I am told, that the problems are so serious that it is a question whether Canada will be able to carry on her full duty in this war, on account of financial matters-I am not going into that part of it, it would not be right to do so.
You could not help but say a mean thing about it, could you?

What has got wrong
with the hon. member?
He is crazy.
Oh no, he is not crazy; he is just devilish. He has these fits every once in a while, and when they come on him it is like a brainstorm.
Not at all.

It is not craziness, it is a brainstorm, and he is not responsible for a short time. But the brainstorm passes away, and after a while-he is a very genial fellow. I was pointing out that the financial affairs of this country were serious, and I do not think we are justified in making an expenditure of a quarter of a million dollars on the ground that it would be of benefit to the locality, as I believe it would. It is just like the expenditure in my own province. While I believe it would be of great 'benefit and should be carried out, I do not think this is the time for it.

The item before us is not for a quarter of a million. The next item item is different. That is the main channel.
Mr. 'CARVELL:	I am not finding the
fault that it would not be a great improvement if carried out, but it does seem to be that, under present conditions and under the policy that has been laid down by the Government, this item should be dropped, and we should not go on with a work of this kind, because if we spend $100,000 this year it will develop into $200,000 or $300,000 next year, and so on.

I agree with the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) that these items are not identical. There are certain lands along the north arm that would become valuable for industries if this dredging were done and a good channel put through there. The next item is for the main channel which is used all the time and stands in a different position from this particular item of $100,000, which I think might well stand for further investigation. The item in reference to the main channel is in a different position. Any necessary repairs to that channel ought to be made.
What will the hon. gentleman say to Mr. Macdonald?
He did not communicate with me on the subject. If I get into the Government I will have my answer ready.

I was at this place and I really think that this main channel work is one that must be carried on. Perhaps I can get some more information about this other item, and let the $100,000 item stand.
Item stands.
Revelstoke-extension of wing dam, $20,000. Mr. REID: This is asked for by District Engineer Ford to build an extension to the
wing dam to divert the main current from flowing over against the wharf, threatening its destruction.
Resolution stands.
Dredging in the provinces of Ontario, Quebec-further amount required, $50,000.
British Columbia-further amount required, $100,000.
Are these items taken every year in addition to the specific items ?
This is required in addition to the amount in the main estimates to carry out dredging at various places in these provinces.
Are these amounts for dredging required to finish up present contracts?
We have plants in all the provinces; this is to carry on the work of the dredges that are being used. Many dredges have been laid up during the last year or two.
Do you intend to keep all the dredges busy?
No.
Are there any dredges along the river St. Clair that are not being used at present and that are available for small works?
The deputy tells me that there is one in that district.
Is there one near Chatham?

Yes, I think there is one there not in operation.
Slides ' and booms-Gatineau river-new boom, $11,000.
Will the minister explain this item?

The present boom has been in use since its construction in 1874. After a long service of over forty-two years, it is not to be depended upon to the same extent as in the past. Each additional season that the old boom is used, the risk will be increased. Some of the timbers are decayed, especially on their outer surface. Others appear to be sound, but altogether the boom shows evidence of having been subjected to severe strain.
Is it possible that the federal Government is providing booms for lumbermen?

The Public Works Department have always provided booms on the

Saguenay, the St. Maurice and the Gatineau rivers. They charge tolls; quite a large revenue comes from the lumber men in respect of these booms.

Even though this practice has been followed for forty-two years, surely it is time for the Government to ask the lumbermen to look after their own booms. 1 do not understand upon what principle the Government of Canada should build booms for lumbermen on ithe Gatineau, the 'St. Maurice or any other river.

This boom was built many years ago. These works were started to help the lumber trade; they have been carried on ever since; there has been no change.
Roads and bridges-new bridge to replace present Union bridge over Ottawa river between Ottawa and Hull, $120,000.
This amount is required to replace the present steel span bridge over the Ottawa river, between Ottawa and Hull.
Where is this bridge?
Between Booth's and Eddy's.
Does the Dominion Government build the bridge in its entirety?
Yes. It is an interprovincial bridge; it was built in 1889 by the^Dominion Government.
The Dominion Government does not build all interprovincial bridges.
They built this one, and now we have to rebuild it,
Does the Dominion Government charge the Street Railway company anything for the use of the bridge?
No.

It is a great thing to live in Ottawa.
M.r. GRAHAM: It is news to me if the Federal Government builds any of these bridges in their entirety. It is very rarely that the Federal Government give aid to an entirely provincial scheme, although it has done so under exceptional circumstances. 'The Federal Parliament has quite frequently granted aid to interprovincial bridges, but here is a case where both provinces are relieved and the federal authority assumes the entire responsibility. If Ottawa and vicinity were made a federal district, as has been suggested, the federal authority would be expected to do this work. But, unless there is some arrangement between 
the province and the federal authority, I cannot see why this Parliament should be asked to pay the entire cost of a bridge between the two provinces.
I agree with the hon. gentleman that, this being an interprovincial bridge, the provinces of Quebec and Ontario should pay for it, assisted, perhaps, by the Dominion Government.
Does this amount cover the whole cost?
Yes. The engineer condemns the bridge, and it is necessary to proceed with a renewal of it at once.

Will the minister make inquiry, and when his estimates come up again give us an explanation of his? This is establishing a precedent; if we build an interprovincial bridge here we could build one elsewhere

I will get the explanation for my hon. friend.
Progress reported.
